maintopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER  REFERENCE TO CANADIAN PRESS REPORT
MR. DIEFENBAKER  REFERENCE TO CANADIAN PRESS REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of a Canadian Press article in last night's Citizen headed "Diefenbaker's Charge Denied" and which reads as follows:
Calgary (CP)-A statement in the Commons that the C.N.R. has hired 1,000 immigrants in the Calgary area while bypassing men previously laid off was denied today by railway officials.
The statement was made Tuesday by John Diefenbaker, Progressive Conservative member of parliament for Prince Albert.
A C.N.R. spokesman said: "We have not hired 1,000 immigrants in the Calgary division-not at all."
The Canadian Press dispatch in question read that I had made the statement:
. . . C.N.R. employees are living in fear of layoffs. In the Calgary area, those laid off were passed over recently when 1,000 immigrants were hired for extra gang work.
My question of privilege is simply this. I never made any such statement at any time. What I did say is reported in Hansard at page 3176:
Strong complaints have been made about R. F. Welch Limited, I think that is the name of the company. Mr. Gordon gave his promise that the things complained of would cease after March 31, but he did not say what year. Since March 31, 1,000 people who have been recently brought into Canada have been placed on two extra gangs out of Calgary, according to my information. What about the men who have been laid off? Why were they not given an opportunity, those who would be fitted for that work, to take this employment? A promise was given by Mr. Gordon that this was going to stop, that the injustices resulting from the hiring agreements of that company would be a thing of the past.
I put the emphasis on the word "that". My reference was to R. F. Welch Limited holding certain contracts with the Canadian National Railways, that this company had recently hired 1,000 men and had not taken into account unemployed section and maintenance men. My point of privilege is that the statement alleged to have been made by me, as reported by the Canadian Press, is not in any way in accordance with the statement I made in the house.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BURNABY, B.C.-ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISH- MENT OF METROPOLITAN AREA
speechtext: should like to address a question to the Acting Postmaster General. Can he make a statement now with respect to the postal situation in East Burnaby, British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Postmaster General):
subtopic: BURNABY, B.C.-ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISH- MENT OF METROPOLITAN AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early this year representations were made to the effect that the Burnaby area should be treated as a postal entity. At the present time, North Burnaby and South Burnaby are served under the jurisdiction of the postmaster, Vancouver; East Burnaby is served under the jurisdiction of the postmaster, New Westminster. It was understood that it was the desire of the people of East Burnaby that they should be served in a similar manner to the people in the rest of Burnaby, namely from Vancouver. Based on this understanding, the department agreed to the change.
This change in service would affect the postage rates charged. At the present time the local letter rate of 4 cents applies to mail between East Burnaby and New Westminster. Under the rearrangement contemplated the rate would be 5 cents, but on the other hand the rate to Vancouver which previously had been 5 cents would be 4 cents.
No sooner had the decision been made public than representations were received from people in East Burnaby objecting to the change. From a practical post office point of view, I am informed, East Burnaby could be served either under the postmaster at Vancouver or the postmaster at New Westminster.
In view of these representations further consideration was given to the question, including representations heretofore made to the effect that there should be one metropolitan postal area comprising the territory
Inquiries of the Ministry served within the letter carrier delivery boundaries of both Vancouver and New Westminster. This would mean that the local letter rate of 4 cents would apply within this whole area.
It has been decided that the most equitable and efficient arrangement would be to establish a metropolitan postal area covering both the Vancouver and New Westminster postal districts. Vancouver and New Westminster will both continue to have post offices described by those names. There need be no change in the method of addressing or handling mails. It is essential, however, that there should appear in the address a positive indication of the locality in which the address is situated, otherwise delays will undoubtedly ensue. East Burnaby will be designated as "Burnaby 3".
The four-cent rate for the area will be effective from May 1, 1955.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 27, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdon-nell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.
(Translation) :

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, agriculture, offshore fishing and lumbering are among the chief means of livelihood of a great many people in the province of Quebec. More particularly in the eastern part, in Gaspe, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, the people are almost entirely dependent upon those three sources
The Budget-Mr. Arsenault
of income to live on or, in some cases, to achieve a modicum of comfort.
Indeed very few farmers of that area earn their living through farming alone, and few fishermen engage exclusively in fishing operations. Therefore, lumbering and the sale of pulpwood constitute a necessary if not indispensable adjunct to the family budget. Those three sources of revenue, sea, land and forest, can be said to constitute the very basis of the economy of the eastern part of the province of Quebec.
Last year, because of bad weather and of the heavy damage done to crops by insects, in various parts of the province, many farmers sustained irretrievable losses. In Gaspe, many of them even lack the necessary seed for this spring. I have received numerous and pathetic appeals for assistance from farm organizations and individual farmers of my constituency. But that problem is not a responsibility of the federal government.
However, due to the urgency of the matter and the pressing needs of the farmers of my county, I feel I must call this situation to the attention of the provincial authorities whose responsibility this is. Let me make clear, though, that these words of mine, and the statements I wish to make in the course of my remarks today, are by no means intended to embarrass the Quebec government.
It is a well known fact that, for several months, the farmers of this country, more particularly those from the province of Quebec, have been expressing alarm over the very important matter of the price of butter. Federal members from that province have received numerous representations in this regard, notably from the officers and members of the Catholic farmers' union. Personally, I have received some 1,400 letters on this subject.
The Quebec members in this house have joined hands in placing those pressing demands before federal authorities. Farmers of that province have thus received renewed proof of the fact that they have good friends here, on whom they can rely in emergencies.
The federal government has attempted to protect the Canadian farmer, and more particularly the farmer from Quebec, from the disastrous effects of a drop in dairy prices.
Price support on butter has once more been fixed at 58 cents a pound.
On behalf of the farmers of my riding, I wish to extend my sincere thanks to the government, in particular to the right hon.

The Budget-Mr. Arsenault
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for this wise decision which will be beneficial not only to farmers but also, indirectly, to everyone in Canada. When agriculture is prosperous, the entire country is also prosperous.
I said that a large part of the population of the province of Quebec earns its living from fishing. I must remind the house, however, that the value of the catch in that province for 1954 was 23 per cent lower than in 1953, and 29 per cent less than in 1952.
For instance, in the province of Quebec 35 million pounds of cod were caught in 1954. This catch, as it came out of the net, was worth $773,000.
In comparison with 1953, the amount of cod caught was 28-5 per cent smaller, the value 15-3 per cent less. A comparison between 1954 and 1952 shows that the amount of cod taken was down 39-5 per cent, and the sums paid to the fishermen, 45 [DOT] 6 per cent.
The herring catch, which had been 28,000 tons in 1952 and 24,000 tons in 1953, was down to 18,000 tons in 1954.
The salmon catch has also been seriously reduced in the last few years. The gradual disappearance of salmon from the Atlantic coast is such as to give rise to the most serious misgivings.
On the other hand, in the Magdalen islands, the total value of the lobster catch was up from $485,000 in 1952 to $703,000 in 1953 and $721,000 in 1954. But that is only one happy exception to the rule, and of no advantage to the other eastern districts of the province of Quebec.
Generally speaking, then, it may be said that in 1954 there was a serious reduction in the revenue of fishermen from the counties of Bonaventure, Gaspe South, Gaspe North, Charlevoix and Saguenay, compared to 1953 and especially to 1952.
Consequently, if on one hand some sections of the eastern part of the province of Quebec met with serious difficulties last year on account of excessive rain and of insects, on the other hand the income from our offshore fishing, especially for the past two years, has been sadly inadequate, and is greatly missed by our people.
The catch and the prices paid to fishermen have dropped so much that the total revenue


of our Quebec sea fisheries is but $2,440,473 compared to $2,706,248 in 1953, and $3,088,448 in 1952.
I said just now that in the eastern part of the province, more particularly in Gaspe and on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, the lumbering industry constitutes a necessary adjunct to the revenue of the people, more especially when farming and fishing fail.
Now, considering the serious conditions in agriculture and offshore fishing, which I just mentioned, farmers and fishermen of the province of Quebec, especially in the eastern district, who own woodlots had reason to expect from the sale of pulpwood a fair return which would have enabled them to support their families. On the contrary, even in that field, they have been shamefully exploited.
Considering the high cost of living, the cost of newsprint both on the national and international market, and the profits revealed in the financial reports of the pulpwood companies which are taking advantage of our natural resources, the ridiculously low prices paid in recent years, and last year in particular for pulpwood in the constituency of Bonaventure in the Gaspe peninsula, and in many other districts in the province of Quebec, are nothing less than an inducement to lawlessness.
I have here the results of investigations conducted during the winter by officers of the Catholic farmers' union in the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe, on prices paid to pulpwood producers in the Gaspe peninsula.
Those investigations show that, in February and March 1955, prices as low as $10.50, $9.50, $8.50 and even $7.50 were being paid in the Gaspe peninsula for a cord of pulpwood delivered to the truck roads.
Do you know how much it costs to fell, saw or "bucksaw", as the lumberjacks say, and cart to the truck roads, often miles away, a cord of pulpwood cut on the average farmer's or settler's lot in the Gaspe peninsula?
Two good men, a good horse and ten hours of work a day are required to do the job.
It costs $2 a day to feed two men, and this is no exaggeration; and for a horse at least $1. For a good horse, the value of a day's work is $3, which makes a total of $6.
That means that when pulpwood is paid $10 a cord, delivered alongside the truck roads, there is left only $4 in net revenue to

be split between two men. It also means that not only do the pulpwood producers in eastern Quebec have to be content with a measly salary of $2 a day, for ten hours of hard work, but they are practically giving their wood away to the shareholders of pulpwood companies, the majority of whom are quite often foreigners.
And when pulpwood is paid $7.50 a cord, alongside the truck roads, as was the case last winter in certain parts of the Gaspe peninsula-and I have proof of it right here-we find, on the basis of the same figures, that those two men net only 75 cents each a day, which amounts to about 7 A cents an hour, on which to raise a large family.
When I see some printers of the Montreal newspaper Le Devoir, who already get a salary of $4,000, $5,000 and $6,000 a year, go on strike, I really wonder what they would do if their situation was that of the woodcutters and the pulpwood producers in the province of Quebec.
Some will say that, with modern equipment -which our woodcutters are not always able to get-two men can cut more than a cord of wood in a day. Of course they can, if this wood is cut on company limits, right in the middle of a virgin forest and close to the river down which the wood is floated. But not so on the woodlots of the farmers and settlers of the Gaspe peninsula, where the trees are sparse and have to be hauled long distances to the truck road during the winter, or even in the mud during the fall and spring.
From 75 cents to $2 a day for a man who works hard, often from morning till night, to raise a large family and try to make both ends meet! And things have come to such a pass in this twentieth century, in a Christian country which is often held up as an example for other countries of the world, in a democratic country which earmarks billions of dollars for the defence of our way of life, of that way of life, and especially in a province which claims to be in the vanguard of the fight against communism.
I say that our woodcutters and settlers in Quebec are not immunized against the seeds of revolutionary and communistic ideas, and I would add that the wonder drug that would immunize them has not yet been found. Let our industrial leaders take heed and consider seriously their responsibilities before it is too late!
The Budget-Mr. Arsenault
For, by enriching the foreigners who are taking advantage of our natural wealth while making capital out of indigence, the suffering and even the despair of our people, we sow the most fertile seed of revolution and communism to be found in the country.
Thus some capitalists, blinded by greed, avarice, or sheer stupidity, are acting as the best promoters of Moscow in our midst.
Communism! They are the ones who, by their unfair practices, arouse communism in the minds and hearts of our people. And unfortunately, those exploiters are beyond the reach of the padlock law.
Our own Canadian forests, the woods of Quebec, our own province and, in particular, those of the Gaspe peninsula, were not created by the Lord for the sole benefit of Thread-needle street, Wall street, Bay street or St. James street.
The lumber industry is one of the most important in the province of Quebec, if not actually the most important. The pulp industry, in particular, is an essential factor of our economic and social structure. It directly affects the standard of living of a large part of our population.
Lest we take for granted that the province of Quebec has become the colonial empire of a few privileged rich men, the development of our natural resources, of our forests, should first and foremost assure the subsistence and welfare of our population in Quebec.
If there is a field in which Quebec should be autonomous, it is that one, for our provincial government has the sole jurisdiction with regard to our forests, and our lumber industry within the province.
As a matter of fact, lease permits either for settlers' lots or wooded lands are granted or refused by the provincial government.
The only authority entitled to grant timber rights to individuals or companies is the provincial government. It is the provincial government that collects cutting fees. It is also the provincial government that has established the ceiling price to be paid by the owners of provincial newspapers for their newsprint by direct representations to the companies. In view of the uncompromising attitude of some pulp companies in their transactions with the lumber producers, and of the extreme unfairness they show to the farmers and settlers of the province of
3248	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Arsenault Quebec, in spite of the solemn warning that was given to them in this very house, by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) and in the very words of the premier of Quebec, I believe it to be the duty of the government of that province to intervene with regard to the establishment of the floor price to be paid the farmers and settlers for their pulp-wood.
The provincial government has the power to fix a maximum price for the newsprint sold to the newspaper publishers of the province. By the same token, it should have the right to fix a minimum price to be paid to settlers and farmers.
Because we live in the province of Quebec we should not have to pay more taxes than elsewhere. Because we live in the province of Quebec we should not be paid lower salaries than elsewhere. Because we are from the province of Quebec we should not be forced to sell our products more cheaply than elsewhere, pulpwood in particular.
This situation, Mr. Speaker, has lasted all too long. There is no reason in the world why a cord of pulpwood cut in Gaspe should not fetch as high a price as a cord of pulpwood cut in Ontario or on the Pacific coast.
I might add that a cord of pulpwood, which often costs as much as $25 to $35 delivered at the mill, when it has been cut on company limits and floated or hauled over long distances, should be worth at least $15 when delivered to truck loading points on roads by our farmers or settlers: not $7.50 nor $8, but $15.
Therefore I say that a minimum price of $15 a cord should be set right away throughout the eastern region of the province for pulpwood bought from farmers, settlers or other producers.
I do not mention any figure for the other parts of the province as I am not familiar with conditions there.
But I do know that since 1952, because pulpwood has been paid from $5 to $7 a cord less than should have been paid to our farmers and settlers, at a time when the price of newsprint kept going up and the profits of pulpwood companies kept piling up, the people of the Gaspe peninsula and of eastern Quebec have been cheated out of some $2 million a year. Thus the benefit of family allowances generously distributed to the families in those regions by the federal


government has, to a large extent, been cancelled out.
Such a highly unjust situation must be met with an immediate remedy. Here is what I should like to suggest:
1.	I propose that the inquiry which the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) has asked the Department of Justice to undertake with respect to the Gatineau valley under the Combines Investigation Act be extended to every region of the province of Quebec and particularly to the Gaspe peninsula.
2.	I respectfully urge the Hon. Maurice Duplessis, premier of the province of Quebec, and the members of his government, to pass an order in council fixing the minimum price to be paid to pulpwood producers in the province of Quebec. Such a minimum price would have to be at least $15 a cord, delivered at a truck loading site, for the eastern part of the province.
3.	As a citizen of the province of Quebec, I respectfully urge the Quebec provincial legislature to adopt at its next session a legislative measure which would empower the minister of lands and forests of the province, among other things, to:
(a)	investigate prices paid to farmers and settlers for pulpwood cut in the province on wooded lands or licenced lots;
(b)	issue regulations governing the establishment of the minimum price to be paid to producers for pulpwood; concerning the measuring of the wood and the quantity of pulpwood to be bought each year from settlers and farmers, taking into account their other sources of supply and their needs;
(c)	issue any other regulation to safeguard the interests of wood producers within the province of Quebec.
Before resuming my seat, I repeat that the remarks I have just made must not be interpreted as an attack either against the wood dealers, or the pulp companies or the provincial government.
I attack nobody in particular and I lay no charge whatsoever against anybody.
I am only stating facts that have lasted long enough, conditions I believe it is my duty to reveal and proclaim, and which I shall denounce and proclaim as long as they have not been efficiently remedied.
As a farmer's son, I know from my own experience how strenuously our men must work to support their families.

I also know, from personal experience, that a lumberman, a farmer, a settler or lumber producer, be he from the Gaspe peninsula, from the north shore of the St. Lawrence or the Gatineau, deserves as fair a compensation for a good day's work as any other Canadian, from any other part of our country, in a similar profession.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on his first budget. I am glad to note that the minister is an optimist, because that is a state of mind that is always good to have in a country like Canada. I hope the gross national product for this year turns out to be as high as his estimate.
As far as the budget is concerned, there have been some tax reductions. While the minister decided to make these reductions in the income tax they really do not amount to very much, as has been pointed out, to the average family. The total saving will be only 40 or 50 cents a week, which I do not think will buy many refrigerators or other appliances.
I suppose we should all be thankful for any reduction in taxation, however small it may be, but the result of this reduction is that those who need a tax reduction most are receiving the least benefit. I refer to those whose incomes are so small that they are not taxable at all. The only way those people can be benefited is by removing the sales tax from essential commodities. I do not suppose that would make any great impression on the mind of the public, at least not as much as a reduction in the income tax even though it is not very large. However, in his next budget the minister may consider removing the sales tax from such commodities, as it will then be a little closer to election time.
There are three aspects of the budget with which I should like to deal briefly. The first is the failure of the minister to remove the sales tax from stationery and other essential supplies used by welfare organizations such as the Red Cross, the cancer society and so on. Representations on behalf of these organizations have been made in this house in other years and on other occasions, and I cannot help but feel that it is perfectly ridiculous for people to donate to these organizations and be able to deduct their donations
The Budget-Mr. Nesbitt from their taxable income, then have the government turn around and make these welfare organizations pay the sales tax on necessary supplies, stationery, advertising material and so on.
The second matter with which I should like to deal concerns the druggists of this country. Representations were made to me earlier this year which I passed on to the minister. I understand that other hon. members and various associations have also made representations to the minister in this regard. In this connection I should like to read a letter which was sent to me by the retail pharmacists' association of Woodstock, a small city in my riding, which I think sets out the situation very cogently and concisely.
Dear Sir,
We the retail pharmacists' association of Woodstock wish to present a brief on a subject which has been causing us increasing concern during the last year or so. In recent months the problem has become increasingly acute and shows every indication of becoming a very real point of contention.
During the last year or so this association has expended considerable time, money and energy to make it practical and advantageous to the medical practitioner and his patient for the doctor to write prescriptions to be dispensed by the pharmacist rather than dispense medicine from his own office.
Our endeavours in this respect have met with considerable success but we now find that we are being stymied to a great extent due to the following situation.
The new modern drugs in use by the medical practitioner are quite expensive, prescriptions running from $5 to $15 are no longer uncommon. If these prescriptions are filled by the doctor in his office, they are deductible as a medical expense for income tax purposes. If however the doctor writes a prescription and it is filled by the pharmacist the patient cannot then claim the cost as a deduction on his income tax.
As a result of this inconsistency we are finding that local doctors in sympathy with their patients who are in need of expensive medication are handing out these medicines in their offices. In addition we have also been advised that patients are asking their doctor to supply expensive medication when required, rather than give them a written prescription for the pharmacist to fill.
We believe the situation as it exists at the present time causes definite discrimination against the pharmacist and that it merits the sincere consideration of the income tax department. Why should the same prescription be income tax deductible when the doctor fills it and not be deductible when the pharmacist fills it?
I omit the remainder of this letter, which is not particularly relevant to the point. The letter is signed:
Woodstock retail pharmacists' association M. A. Bernath, president Gordon Reinhart, secretary
I do not think it is necessary for me to make any further comment on this matter, as I think it has been expressed neatly in this
3250	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nesbitt letter of the association. I hope the Minister of Finance will consider this matter, if not this year then perhaps next year.
The third item with which I should like to deal refers to the present monetary situation in the country, under which prices are decidedly inflated. I want to refer to the effects of these inflated price levels upon older persons who are in receipt of relatively small pensions, or who are living on small fixed incomes. I think all hon. members realize that elderly people, whether they be living on small fixed incomes or on pensions, cannot save very much with the present prices of necessities such as food, clothing and so on.
These high prices also affect young married couples, who quite often find it impossible to save anything. I notice in an article in the paper the other day that instalment buying is at the highest level in the history of the Dominion of Canada. I submit that this practice has been aided and abetted by the government. I do not say that it is necessarily wrong, but the buying of N.H.A. houses, war veterans housing and so on on the instalment plan gets people into the habit. When people buy houses under these plans they find they need furniture, and that is also bought on the instalment plan. Then they need a television set and a car and everything else.
In a country as wealthy as Canada people are entitled to these things. As things are at the present time they have to buy them on the instalment plan or wait perhaps 50 or 60 years before being able to buy a car or some furniture which they would like to have. It may be extravagant, but these young people feel that they should have these things if at all possible. As a result of this instalment buying many young married couples are not able to save any substantial amount of money for a rainy day, and things are still worse should the breadwinner happen to die.
There are a number of hon. members in this house who are in the legal profession. I am quite sure many of those hon. members will have come in contact with that situation as I have myself. Dependents of elderly persons and dependents of young married persons who die are often left destitute, except for the various public welfare schemes which the provincial and federal governments have in force. Very often you have a young married man-it does not occur too often, fortunately, but I have seen such cases-who belongs to a lodge. The lodge may pay funeral expenses; it may be one of these mutual benefit schemes. Then the wife and two or three children are left with the


house, and a great many instalments to pay on it and the furniture, the car, and the television set. They are left with instalments to meet every month and no money to do it with except family allowances or, in certain provinces such as the province of Ontario, mothers' allowance.
That is hardly a desirable situation. Not only does it occur with young people but, as I have mentioned before, it occurs with elderly people who have been unable to save too much and who have retired on small fixed incomes and on pensions. To help this situation I suggest for the consideration of the minister that premiums on straight life insurance policies up to $10,000-that is the amount of the policy, not the premium-if these policies are payable directly or indirectly to the dependents as defined under the Income Tax Act, that such premiums be allowed as a deduction from the taxable income.
Statistics are difficult to obtain with regard to the number of life insurance policyholders in Canada, and it is impossible at the present time to obtain statistics with regard to the types of life insurance the policyholders hold, whether it is term insurance, straight insurance, twenty-pay life or some other form. It is also impossible at the present time to find out how many heads of families are policyholders. The department of insurance and the dominion bureau of statistics have no statistics available in this respect.
However, I was able to obtain some figures on this matter. It appears that Mr. A. Bruce Matthews, president of the Canadian Life Insurance Officers Association, in a recent statement set out that there were approximately 5,500,000 life insurance policyholders in Canada at the end of 1954. This is out of a population of 15 million. It must be remembered that by no means all those policyholders are heads of families. They are married women, very often, and very frequently young children have policies put on their lives at an early age in order to get the lower premium, and so on.
I have some further figures that I think are relevant. In 1951-and these figures are in the 1954 Canada Year Book-Canada had a population of approximately 13,600,000. In that total population there were 3,287,384 heads of families. In 1955, with the increase of our population to approximately 15 million, the number of heads of families must have been increased considerably. As a result of these figures the conclusion that must almost necessarily follow-and it is the opinion of various life insurance executives with whom I have talked, both senior and junior-that

there must be a great many heads of families in Canada at the present time who do not carry any type of life insurance.
Another point that is interesting in this regard is that in 1951 the median income for the head of the family in Canada was $2,345. As most hon. members know, the median is a type of average. It is not an arithmetical or geometric average, but it is the picking of a figure out of the centre of a group of other figures. It is a type of average. In any event, as I say, in 1951 the median income for the head of a family in Canada was $2,345. This figure again was obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics. If that is the median income of the head of the family in Canada, it hardly allows for much saving with the present high rents, cost of consumer goods, and so on.
The normal cost-and when I say "normal cost" it does not envisage any unusual situation as to health, occupation or anything of that nature-of $10,000 of straight life insurance for a man age 30 is $213 a year in premium; at age 35 it is $250; at age 40 it is $294. For younger people, of course, it would be less and for an older person it would increase proportionately. If this amount were allowed as a deduction from taxable income, I do not think it would make a great deal of difference in the revenue which the government would have, but it would undoubtedly encourage the purchase of life insurance by people who should have it.
If the breadwinner of the family should die, $10,000 would protect the family for a considerable time and would save them immediate financial embarrassment. That is only the immediate effect. It would also give the dependents a much greater measure of security for the future, and it would cut down certain public welfare charges such as mothers' allowances and so on.
In addition to that-and most important of all, in my opinion-if when the breadwinner died the family were to get $10,000 plus family allowance in some cases, or the old age pension at the other end of the scale, this would make the difference between bare subsistence, as is the situation at the present time in many cases, and moderately comfortable living such as the families of our young married people and our old people deserve.
If the government or rather the minister should, as I have suggested, under the conditions I have suggested, allow insurance premiums on policies to $10,000 to be deducted from taxable income, I am not suggesting for a minute that everybody would go out and buy life insurance, but I certainly think it would encourage them to do so.
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot If the minister would consider doing this at some future time, I should like to see it tried. I think it would help to remedy a situation that needs to be remedied.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with hon. members who have congratulated the Minister of Finance on his budget. He has done exceptionally well, and his budget has been received by the press and by the people of Canada as a good budget which gives hope to the businessmen and all the people of this country.
The accomplishments of the government are so numerous and so vast, Mr. Speaker, that it would take a long time to touch on each subject. There is, however, a matter with which I should like to deal today. I refer to the social legislation of the government, which is improved at every session. Few people realize what great sums of money are paid each year by three departments, namely the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the unemployment insurance commission which comes under the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). For instance, the amounts in the estimates for the
current year are as follows:
1.	National health and welfare .. $ 849,736,017
2.	Veterans affairs	 234,477,896
3.	Unemployment insurance
(benefits paid to claimants) ____ 174,730,279
Total expenditure	 $1,238,944,192
These figures mean that each year the government is spending much more than a billion dollars in pensions and their administration. I wish to pay special attention to the welfare division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The national health branch of that department spends $56,229,456. The welfare branch has a much heavier expenditure of $785,241,681, and for civil defence there is an amount of $7,001,024, making a total of $848,472,161. This does not include costs of administration.
With regard to family allowances, the amount in the estimates is $383 million. For old age security payments there is $367,600,000, for old age assistance $22,100,000, for blind persons' allowances $3 million, and for disabled persons' allowances $6 million. The increases in 1955-56 over 1954-55 are $17,600,000 for family allowances, $11,750,000 for old age security payments, $500,000 for old age assistance and $6 million for disabled persons' allowances, making a total increase of $35,850,000 this year over last year. This includes allowances to disabled persons who are very dear to my heart, because I deeply sympathize with those who have suffered

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
so much that they are invalids and cannot live normal lives. I congratulate the minister and the government on reaching an understanding with the provinces to pay pensions to invalids.
The amount of $35,850,000 represents the increase this year over last year. As I said before, the total expenditure of the Department of National Health and Welfare is nearly $850 million this year. It will be more than that with the supplementary estimates which will come before us before the end of the session.
In March, 1954, there were 4,942,044 children receiving family allowances. It is enormous when we think of it. In my county, for instance, the amount paid each year to the mothers for their children is about $2 million. There are 686,127 old age security pensioners in Canada, 93,273 old age assistance recipients and 8,214 people receiving blind persons' allowances. This means that in this country there are 5,729,658 people receiving a pension of some sort out of a total population of some 15 million people, and this figure does not include the disabled persons who have only been receiving allowances for a short time.
The government deserves to be warmly congratulated for having understood that in these years of the progress of human understanding it is necessary for the government to divide the wealth of the country in such a way that the less fortunate may have an opportunity to enjoy the comforts of life. To what extent? The extent is limited by the ability of the taxpayers to pay. And this is not all. This is the share of the federal government in a certain field where the provinces make other expenditures.
For instance, family allowances to mothers for their young children under 16 are paid entirely by the federal government at Ottawa. Old age pensions are paid 50-50 by the federal government and the provinces. Allowances to the blind are paid 75 per cent by Ottawa and 25 per cent by the provinces. Out of each dollar paid to the old people and the blind Ottawa pays more than 91 cents. Pensions to the disabled will be paid 50 per cent by Ottawa and 50 per cent by the provinces. Pensions for people 70 years of age and over are entirely paid by Ottawa, and the allowances paid to those between 65 and 70 are paid half by the provinces and half by Ottawa.
I am very pleased that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has been successful in reaching an agreement with the provinces respecting the payment of allowances to disabled persons or invalids. It is important to note that these


pensions are administered and paid by the provinces, who then receive a refund of half the amount of the pension from Ottawa after it is paid. This is a very considerable expenditure.
I am not so very old, but I remember the time when there were no old age pensions or family allowances. There was nothing of that kind. It is not only that the provinces are doing their share. They pay a certain proportion of the old age pension, of the pensions for invalids and for the blind. They pay a pension also to needy mothers, and they pay a lot in workmen's compensation. They have many other social undertakings which are very helpful to the people of Canada. I am very glad that the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces are working hand in hand to improve the social conditions and health of the Canadian people. Naturally it cannot all be done at one time.
Twenty-five years ago, when old age pensions were first introduced in this house, nobody would have believed that needy people between 65 and 70 would receive a pension. They would have raised their shoulders if one had told them that nearly five million children would receive family allowances. They never would have believed it. They would have found it incredible. To the blind we are most sympathetic, but it took some time to get pensions for the blind. Their case was argued in the house and in the press and people were sympathetic to them, but it was done gradually. We have reached a point unequalled in any country in the world. There is no country that has as complete social legislation as Canada has.
I congratulate very warmly my neighbour and friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who has worked so hard to have his point of view accepted by the government and by this house. I am very proud of him and of the officials of the health department of Quebec, especially Dr. Jean Gregoire and Dr. J. C. Beaudet, whom I know very well. Dr. Beaudet was with the health unit at Riviere du Loup before becoming assistant deputy minister in Quebec city. They have done a lot for the people of our province. I am not going to dwell on that because I want to speak particularly about the welfare side of the question. I am not so familiar with the welfare department in Quebec, but it has come to my knowledge that there are many cases in which they have done well for people who were ill.
Now, sir, what I have said is something that is general knowledge. What the government has done has not been done for political purposes, but it has been done in the good Samaritan way, just to give a hand to the

needy; to the mothers of large families; to old Canadians who had the benefit of long lives and who needed some support in their old age; to the blind, who deserve every consideration; and to the invalids. Perhaps the invalids should have been looked after earlier, but better late than never. In this case the amount paid in family allowances and old age pensions was so high it was impossible to do it all at once. All this deserves special consideration.
I am greatly surprised when some people who are heartless, who are intriguers, use propaganda to try to double the old age pension. This is a thing I cannot understand. I am in favour of as high an amount as possible being paid to the mothers of large families. Everybody is. But there is a limit that cannot be exceeded, and it is the ability of the taxpayer to meet the expenditures. Very often we have suggestions from gentlemen who want certain large expenditures made but who, at the same time, ask for a reduction in taxes. This is a thing I have never understood.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question, Mr. Speaker? Would he not have said that during the war, when the proposal was first made to introduce family allowances, it might have been argued that Canada was at war and we could not consider introducing family allowances? Would the member comment on that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, during the war the expenditure was so large that it was unbelievable, and the purpose of the war expenditure was to protect not only Canadian children but all the Canadian people from attacks by the enemy. This was why all the money spent during the war was used for that purpose. Unfortunately the allowance was delayed. I regretted that. But if my hon. friend looks at Hansard he will see that I, along with others, made speeches in favour of this measure. I refer to the hon. members for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Blanchette) and for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand). It was because of the repetition of our requests that finally it was granted. I must remind the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) also that the thing that touched me very deeply was the very kind words of the minister in the house, when he said that I had been among those members who had insisted the most upon pensions for invalids.
All this has been done, and as I have said it comes gradually. Is it possible to increase it? My hon. friend says yes. Perhaps he is right. He is right if he finds expenditures that can be dropped or new taxes that can be imposed on the Canadian people. If he
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
found new taxes that were popular and that would be accepted by the Canadian people, he could increase the family allowances; otherwise he could not. If he thinks about it he will realize the soundness of my argument. The government is well disposed to give assistance to large families. There is no discussion about it. On the other hand the government cannot impose taxation so heavy that it would destroy trade and business in Canada. If we are to have revenue it must come from business in general, and business must prosper if we are to be able to pay taxation.
It is a very difficult problem, and my hon. friends should be careful when they are discussing it. There are some people who make a comparison between the indemnity of $8,000 plus the $2,000 for expenses paid to members of parliament and the amounts paid for family allowances, old age pensions and things of that kind. In the first place the indemnity of $10,000-and this sum includes the expenses-paid to members of parliament represents so small a fraction of the money spent for social welfare purposes that it is quite infinitesimal. But we do not hide it. We accept the $10,000. Are we worth it or not? That is for the people to judge. The amount of salary paid to anyone out of public moneys is not like the ages of women. It can be known; it can be disclosed. I feel no shame when I go tomorrow to get my cheque, because most of it I spend among my constituents. They get the money, and that must be the same with all hon. members.
There are some persons who agitate that the indemnities paid to members of parliament are too high. But what do they receive, themselves? I would refer to Turnon des electeurs de la province de Quebec, the Quebec Social Crediters. I call them crazy; they abuse me, but it makes no difference. Very often when I drive along in my car small dogs bark as the car passes, but they do not follow the dust of the car very long. And I attach no more importance to it than that. But when I see members of municipal councils who are credulous enough to send me resolutions prepared by impostors, asking that we double family allowances without increasing taxation-well, I say this is the time to tell them to stop. It is the time to open the eyes of the people, and I am going to do so.
I say that the editor of the monthly Vers Demain and la cantiniere are exploiters of public credulity. They are impostors. Their idea is not at all-and I wish to be well understood when I say this-to have family allowances doubled; it is to double the circulation of their papers, which is something

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
entirely different. And I have some proof of this. One of the conquerors was silly enough to send me the receipt he gives to those who subscribed to Vers Demain. Naturally it is yellow. The ordinary subscription to the paper is $2, or 24 months for $4; and if one wants to become a member of the chamber of Social Credit, it is $10 a year. They get that money.
A highly respected gentleman in the province of Quebec, Mr. Abel Marion, president of the Catholic farmers' union, has authorized me to tell the house that once he held meetings at La Sarre and Abitibi, at which there were some white caps present to make trouble. He canned them, tamed them, by telling them, "We have come here to render our accounts. You never have any accounts rendered to you by the heads of l'union des electeurs de la province de Quebec, and there is not only a subscription to the paper but there are also the collections taken after each meeting."
Where do the collections go? I do not know, but it is easy to guess, when we think that some years ago the editor of Vers Demain lost his bank book and there was $41,000 in it to his credit-collections for Vers Demain, collections from the credulity of the naive people who are silly enough to give them money. It goes to support la cantiniere or Vers Demain. That is a fine scheme; it is a racket.
They behave like the witnesses of Jehovah. They have the same tactics, and that is the reason I tell them to get out of my office. They came, just as the witnesses of Jehovah came; so much so that when I saw an old man with his white cap coming to my office I said, "Are you a witness of Jehovah?" He said, "No, I am a Social Crediter from Quebec." I said, "Well, I understand there is no difference between them."
To prove that I am right I shall go one step further. In L'Action Catholique of March 23 last it is stated that the Social Crediters of Quebec, I mean the white caps-who have nothing in common with my hon. friends from Alberta-met together to honour the editor of the monthly, Vers Demain, on the occasion of his 70th birthday anniversary with 500 new subscriptions to that paper. It was a gift. And what was the reason for the gift? The reason was that it is the purpose of l'union des electeurs to have 100,000 subscribers to Vers Demain. But it fell flat. They did not have as many as that. It fell so flat that some of the conquerors have resigned. They told Louis Even and Gilberte Cote that it was a racket, and that they were not going to belong to it any longer, with the


result that they have lost rather than increased subscribers. In one of the last editions there is a figure of 4,025 new subscriptions. It is a fake; it is untrue. Did they lose 4,000? Perhaps but they surely did not gain 4,025, because I was credibly informed that subscriptions to the monthly Vers Demain are on the downgrade.
I regret very much that some otherwise intelligent men who happen to be honoured by the confidence of those who have the right to vote in municipal elections have shown their credulity to the point of passing resolutions suggesting to the government that they should double family allowances without increasing taxation. That is beyond me. I told them I presumed that next fall when they come they will not collect any money from the taxpayers of the municipality; they will find some money; they will get a recipe from Vers Demain to pay taxes without collecting anything from the taxpayers of the municipality.
Sir, I have been in politics a long time. As I said the other day, I have been very much abused. Sometimes I was praised, whether I deserved it or not. I have done my duty. I have done my duty to my constituents, and when I thought something was wrong I told them that I thought it was wrong, subject to listening anew to their point of view. The people cannot be fooled indefinitely. They have been fooled to a certain extent by that paper. Those who belong to that party have made fools of themselves by masquerading the whole year round. It did not bring them success. They have realized one thing, namely that the more they abuse the member for Temiscouata the less success they have. They are like a snake that destroyed its teeth by biting a file; and they will not be the better, they will be the worse for it.
In conclusion, sir, I wish to thank hon. members for their attention and to ask them to think about the large amounts of money that are spent by the government for the benefit of all Canadians of every party, of every race, to improve the conditions under which they live. This is the right way to serve the Canadian people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before turning to the subject matter of the budget I should like to compliment the government on the preliminary federal-provincial conference which ended yesterday. Notwithstanding the fact that for two or three years we have been pressing for such a conference, I am quite sure that all sections of the community across Canada will be pleased that at long last the first steps toward calling a general conference have been taken. The

very fact that top-ranking politicians in this country from five different political parties could sit down together with so much amity and agreement is an indication that we have come a long way since 1945. Some of our provincial governments certainly seem to have outgrown the somewhat childish attitude which they adopted at the conference of 1945, an attitude which said, in effect, "if you do not agree with me I will not play in your back yard."
It is very encouraging to find that in 1955 representatives of all 10 provincial governments can sit down with the representatives of the federal government and reach at least some tentative agreement. I think everyone agrees that the exclusion of the question of unemployment relief from the agenda of the October conference is a move in the right direction. We all certainly hope that before the October conference is called some agreement will have been reached under which the provinces and the federal government between them may take care of the relief of those who are unemployed.
Several features of that conference are commendable. I was particularly happy to read in the Globe and Mail that the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated to the conference that the federal government would be willing to go along with the provinces on a national health insurance scheme, provided that the majority of the provinces-I suppose a majority would mean six including one of the two large provinces would agree on such a scheme. That certainly is an advance on anything we have heard in this house on the matter of national health insurance. It would appear, Mr. Speaker, that dawn is at last breaking on that long Liberal night which began back in 1919, when national health insurance first became a part of the policy of the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thirty-six years is a long night.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is true, as the minister has informed us on a number of occasions, that these things cannot all be done overnight, but that long night would seem to be coming to an end.
There will be fairly general approval of the five topics which it has been agreed to place on the agenda of the October conference. The best we can hope is that such agreements as are reached at that conference will not be too narrow and too late to boost the sagging economy of this country.
If I may turn to the budget itself, I wish first of all to say that there are some commendable points in it. I disagree with those
28, 1955
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
speakers from the official opposition who could find nothing whatever to commend in the budget, who insisted that nothing in the budget would do much good. We all welcome the reduction in the income tax, such as it is. I must point out, however, as did the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that the minister's statement on budget night, as recorded at page 2735 of Hansard, seemed to inspire a little more optimism than was warranted. He told us, for instance, that the new schedule would reduce the tax payable by 12 to 13 per cent for 85 per cent of our taxpayers. That sounds pretty good, that 85 per cent of our taxpayers should get a reduction of from 12 to 13 per cent in their taxes. A little later on, as reported on page 2735 of Hansard he said:
Every married taxpayer with an income up to about $5,000 will get about a 12 per cent reduction. The rate of reduction beyond this point drops of! gradually until it reaches 2-8 per cent at the highest income levels.
That would seem to indicate that the budget was weighted in favour of those in the lower income groups, but if we look at the tables placed on Hansard by the minister, which appear at pages 2736 and 2737, we find that the picture is not too rosy for the taxpayer in the lower income groups. According to those figures, in the year 1955 the single taxpayer earning $2,000 will have a saving of $10; the single taxpayer with an income of $3,000 will have a saving of $20 in his taxes, and the single taxpayer in the $5,000 bracket will have a saving of $40.
The married taxpayers without children with incomes of $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 will have savings of $10, $20, and $30 respectively in 1955. The married taxpayers with two children in the same categories of $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 will have savings in 1955 of $7, $17 and $27 respectively. I merely wanted to call attention to that fact in passing. Small as the reduction is, it will be welcomed by the taxpayers across this country.
The 5 per cent reduction in the excise tax on cars will also be welcomed, and I am sure that the reduction of 2 per cent in the corporation tax on profits over $20,000 will be welcomed by the corporations. I gather from the speeches made by representatives of the official opposition that they would have welcomed a much larger reduction in the corporation tax. As far as I am concerned, and as far as members of this group are concerned-I speak now for the present C.C.F. group of 23-we question the necessity for any reduction in corporation taxes at this time, particularly when we note from the balance sheets of the corporations how good 1954 was for most of them.
3256	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
We in this group approve of budgeting for a deficit. When I spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I suggested that the government should follow the policy they had laid down in their white paper in 1945. At that time they indicated that while it was a good policy to budget for a surplus in prosperous years, it would be good business to budget for a deficit when the economy began to slow down.
We approve also of the notice given in the budget speech that a royal commission will be appointed to study the economic position of our country. We have long advocated economic planning, and if this royal commission means anything it means that the government at last has reached the conclusion that there must be some economic planning in our public affairs and government policy.
I was rather intrigued by the number of Conservative speakers who criticized the government because they have no economic plan at the present time, and who indicated that they thought the setting up of this royal commission was an admission on the part of the government that they had no such plan. This is the first time in my public life that I have known or learned that economic planning was part of the Conservative program as well as that of the Liberals. However, we welcome it regardless of from what corner of the house it comes.
I rise on this occasion to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood and the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, the leader of this C.C.F. group. It might be well to remind ourselves of the nature of those amendments. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood will be found on page 2954 of Hansard of April 19. It reads:
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in its budget proposals the government has failed:
(a)	to give effective stimulus to Canadian enterprise to create employment and opportunity;
(b)	to reduce taxation affecting those on low income and allowances;
(c)	to curb its own extravagance and inefficiency;
(d)	to recognize the serious position in which the Canadian farmer and other producers now find themselves."
The amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, as reported on page 2958 of Hansard, reads:
That the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:
"(e) to provide assistance to the provincial governments in order to enable them to plan their financing in such a manner as to relieve the people of this country from the crushing load of heavy municipal taxation."


While we support the amendment moved by the official opposition we do so without committing ourselves to the support of the methods suggested by official opposition speakers to implement the policy enunciated in that amendment.
From speeches by the official opposition I tried to find just what they meant by "effective stimulus to Canadian enterprise to create employment and opportunity". I went, of course, to the speech of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees). He holds an extremely important position in the Conservative party. I find that the hon. member for Broadview does not think that the income tax reductions will do anything to stimulate purchasing of our surplus goods and that he thinks that the reduction in the corporation tax is not enough to cause companies to embark on a capital expansion program, indicating that he would like to see a much greater corporation tax reduction.
Much to my surprise, he pointed out that the 2 per cent reduction in corporation tax- that is a reduction from 47 per cent to 45 per cent; in reality it amounts to about a 4 per cent total reduction-will not be passed on to consumers in the form of lower prices. That statement was a bit surprising to me. It was surprising to me that the national president of the Conservative association should have lost faith in private enterprise to the extent that he now does not believe that the corporations of this country will pass on the benefit of their tax reduction to the consuming public in the form of lower prices. If that is so, I just do not know on what logic he bases his appeal for a still larger reduction in corporation taxes.
Then on the question of the royal commission, the hon. member for Broadview was critical of the fact that the government has no economic plan. He went on to say that if the government had had its various departments gathering all this information during the past ten years, they would now have an economic plan. As I said before, we welcome the thought that at long last not only the Liberal party but also the Conservative party has come around to the adoption of that plank in the C.C.F. program which has always been a major one, namely that of economic planning in government.
Then apparently another one of the stimuli which governments could give, according to the member for Broadview, is to take some measures to lower the cost of products we manufacture. From a Conservative whose party supports private enterprise, and who is so critical of government interference with business in any form, this is a surprising suggestion. One wonders what the government

can do to lower the cost of the products that we manufacture without interfering with or exercising some control over industry, as we in the C.C.F. have long suggested.
Then another Conservative stimulus is to take some measures to ensure that more of our primary products are processed in Canada. I do not know how this stimulus can be provided by a government or a party that does not believe in interfering with private enterprise, that does not believe in the government's participation in industry or business or that does not believe in the exercise of any control by government. I just do not see how such governments or such parties can provide the kind of stimulus that is suggested by Conservative speakers for the improvement of our economic condition.
Most of those who have spoken in the debate have offered the government advice. I suppose a little more advice at this stage of the debate will do no more harm and probably no more good than most of the other advice that has come from this side of the house. I suggest-and on this I think all parties are agreed-that the condition of employment in this country is one that requires study. I say "employment", because I think the provision of employment is our No. 1 problem. I think we must think in terms of employment rather than in terms of unemployment. I think we must take the positive attitude or the positive approach and consider ways and means of providing more jobs for more people for longer periods of time.
This country just cannot afford the luxury of having 600,000 people looking for jobs and unable to find them or 600,000 people registered with our unemployment insurance commission. The waste of that manpower is a luxury that we cannot afford. Certainly it represents a condition that should engage the most serious attention of all of us, regardless of our party affiliations. The workers were told that, if they wanted increased wages, they must increase production. For some years since the war the emphasis has been on increasing production. We have been increasing production. We have increased production to the point where, in many lines, we now have more goods than we can dispose of. We have inventories piling up. We have factories laying off help and men going idle. We have reached the point where we have carried increases in production so far that we now have 600,000 unemployed. There are those who advocate, as did the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), that one of the remedies for that is a reduction in the price of commodities and the cost of production. There are those who blame our having a surplus of commodities which we 50433-206
28, 1955
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
cannot dispose of on the fact that we have priced ourselves out of the market and who say that lower prices would be the remedy.
I am sure those of us who lived through the thirties must realize that if the thirties taught us anything they taught us that the lowering of prices alone is not enough to remedy the kind of economic situation in which the country then was and which we are in danger of falling into again. If lowering prices was the answer to the problem, we had the answer in the 1930's. Goodness knows, prices were low enough. We must, as I have said, find some way of creating more jobs for more people, and since industry, and the manufacturing industry in particular, employs the majority of our workers we must find some means of making more jobs for more workers in more factories in this country.
There are those of course who believe that this matter should be left entirely to private enterprise, that it is not the business of the government to get into the construction field, for instance, in competition with private enterprise. I would merely point out that when the necessities of war showed that private enterprise was unable to fill the bill required of it the government, with the approval and support of electors all across the country, stepped into the breach and did not hesitate to direct and control those industries whose products were needed for war but with respect to which private enterprise had failed to fill the bill. Whether in the production of war machines, munitions, ships or whatever it was, when private enterprise failed to meet the needs of the times the government, with the approval of the Canadian public, as I said, entered into the particular field and took steps to see that those needs were met.
Today private enterprise has failed to employ all our people, or perhaps I should say that private enterprise and governments combined have failed to employ all our people with the result that we now have 600,000 unemployed. Does that not seem sufficient justification and reason for the government to undertake at this time a large-scale public works program to supplement the efforts of private enterprise, to create more jobs where private enterprise is failing to create them? It is true that some public works contribute very little to employment. I suppose the experience of the Ontario government in the past year has shown that highway construction, for instance, provides more profits for contractors than it does work for the unemployed.
But there are fields the government can enter which will provide many jobs. We need a trans-Canada highway. We have been working on the project now for some years. The

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
federal government has made a very generous offer to the provinces but the provinces are having difficulty with the construction of the trans-Canada highway. Some are finding the cost of construction per mile too high for them to bear under the present arrangement. Some are finding that to put their money into the construction of the trans-Canada highway will result in the neglect of many other highways in the province. I suggest this is a good time for the government to increase its share of the cost of the trans-Canada highway in order to offset the high construction costs that are slowing up the building of the highway in various provinces. That will not only speed up the construction of the highway with resulting improvement throughout the country, but it will also help to take care to some extent of the waste of manpower taking place in the country at the present time.
There are other fields. There is the question of railway grade crossings. While we commend the government for the increased support it is giving to the railway grade crossing fund, we think there is room for a still further increase in the contribution to the fund so that a very sizeable crossing improvement program can be undertaken throughout Canada. There again we would be doing something that would be useful, something that would result in saving lives, that would improve the transportation system of our country and would also be of some assistance in relieving the unemployment situation.
The third proposal, to mention only three, is that introduced in the house by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) and emphasized by numerous speakers on both sides of the house, the initiation of a broad, imaginative plan for the building of low rental houses. If there is any one field in which the government can assist in meeting the unemployment problem, it is in the building of houses.
While Central Mortgage and Housing has done a reasonably good job within the limits of the regulations by which they are governed, the fact is that the houses which are built are beyond the reach of the people who most need houses. Today it is just as difficult for a family with four, five, or six children to find a home in Toronto as it has been at any time within the past 10 years. When a family is ejected in the city of Toronto today, it is just hopeless for that family to try to find a house that they can rent. There is a great need across this country for the kind of housing scheme that will provide houses on a large scale at a price that those in the lower income groups can rent or buy.


While speaking of a public works program, I trust that when the conference meets in the fall, and when the question of public investment and the development of our natural resources comes before that conference, some arrangement will be made and some agreement reached on the kind of public works that should be undertaken across Canada, the kind of public works in which the federal and provincial governments may unite for the good of the people of Canada. If any of these projects are to be of any use before another winter's unemployment is upon us, then we must take steps now to plan the nature of those projects, and all the preliminary matters that must be settled before the contracts can be let. It is of extreme importance that we waste no time in getting on with a public works program, at both the federal and the provincial levels, with projects of such a nature that the federal and provincial governments may combine their resources.
Another point I think that we should consider-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall conclude then, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry I did not watch the clock. I shall conclude by suggesting that anything we can do to increase the purchasing power of the masses of the people, by an increase in the personal income tax exemption, by an increase in social security benefits, disability pensions, guidance allowances for the blind or anything of that kind, will help us in our present emergency. I trust that the government will not wait until fall to take some forward steps to prevent this country from falling into the condition that harassed us during the thirties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And none more than Harris.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to take part in this debate at this time because traditionally the debate on the budget, like that on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, permits a member to range rather widely and introduce a number of topics in the one speech. Before I address myself to matters relating to the budget, I feel it is necessary to comment upon the extraordinary statement made, first by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson) and later, in similar language, by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis), concerning tax reductions as proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris).

On page 3084 of Hansard for April 22, 1955, in the second column, I find this:
The minister touted the income tax reductions and pointed out how they ranged from 13-3 per cent for those in the lower income tax brackets to 2-8 per cent for those in the higher brackets.-
This is the statement which caused some of us in this corner a little concern.
-when actually it was a 2 per cent reduction across the board. The minister placed the mirage at a distance in the hope that by the time the people became aware of the results, the matters would be forgotten.
Then, in the next paragraph I find this:
Indeed it is nothing but deception to tell the people of Canada they are being given a tax reduction of 13-3 per cent when the tax reduction is 2 per cent and ranges in amount from $5 to $7 to $40.
The same day, a little later, the hon. member for Regina City made a similar statement on page 3113. He said:
I wonder who the government thought they were fooling with that sort of subterfuge. No matter how you figure it out it means a 2 per cent blanket reduction across the board. The government brought this in in a deceptive manner and tried to convey the impression that there was some fairness and equity in the manner in which these reductions were being made, when all the time there was plain evidence that the income tax reductions amounted to a flat 2 per cent reduction across the board.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I point to the similarity of the statements, and there are two things to which I object. The first is the suggestion of deception and the second is that the arithmetic is quite wrong. I am sure that, at least in recent years, the education of the Canadian people has reached a point where they can do a simple problem in percentages. The example that both gentlemen used was that of a married man with two children, the first having an income of $3,000, and the second man having an income of $20,000. The first will get a reduction of $14 and the second of $354. The point is, a reduction from what? In the first case it is a reduction of $14 from $105, which is the amount to be paid in 1954. This is a reduction of 13.3 per cent because $14 is 13.3 per cent of $105. In the second case it is a reduction of $354 from $5,375, which is 6.6 per cent.
I might suggest that the hon. members have mistaken what the minister said, and I therefore refer to page 2735 of Hansard for April 5. These are the words the minister used:
The method by which this result will be reached is to reduce the rates of tax payable on each bracket of income by 2 percentage points.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is a vast difference between a reduction of two percentage points in each bracket of income and a straight 2 per cent across the board. Had it been a straight 2 per cent reduction 50433-206J
The Budget-Mr. Fairey
across the board, the reduction would be of course $2.08 rather than $14, because 2 per cent of $105 is $2.08. And in the second place the reduction would have been $107.50 instead of $354.
I have no quarrel whatever with the statement of both hon. gentlemen, that the minister might have achieved similar or perhaps better results in another way. That is a matter of opinion. But as an old schoolmaster I could not allow that bad calculation to go without comment; because it is likely that these speeches will receive rather wide circulation, and I thought it necessary to make the correction. As for the rhetorical question, whom the government were fooling-well, I will leave that to the Canadian people. I do not think they were trying to fool anybody, except perhaps the two hon. gentlemen.
Now a few words about the budget itself. In my opinion it is a good budget. The minister has been bold enough to reduce taxes, which will result in a sum of money approaching $200 million being added as extra purchasing power in the hands of the public. That is what hon. members on both sides of the house have been asking for. Naturally it will result in increased spending, chiefly on consumer goods. The boldness on the part of the minister and of the government will I think generate confidence and thus encourage investment and the expansion of industry. And if these results ensue, the resulting expansion in industry must in itself stimulate employment.
It was my hope that the minister would find it possible to reconsider, as a special case, the problem of the retail automobile dealers. In this regard I add my support to the views already expressed by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck). In my opinion, because of the policy of manufacturers, the retail automobile dealers find themselves in a position which they cannot avoid by any action they themselves may take. Although I know perfectly well that the government is on very dangerous ground when exceptions are suggested, I do feel there is strong justification for the claim of the automobile dealers for a rebate of the excise tax paid on cars which were not sold at the time the reduction was announced. I do think, though, that the remedy lies within the industry itself. They have anticipated this kind of thing for some years past and, in my opinion, they should have worked out some way to avoid this difficulty. Surely the manufacturers and the retail dealers can devise some method by which dealers stand neither to gain nor to lose, owing to changes in excise tax rates. In the meantime I hope
3260	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fairey
the minister will take not a second look- but, perhaps it may be, a twenty-second look.
Then, something about Canada's future: We all have great confidence in Canada, and believe that we are now on the threshold of a great industrial expansion. In all provinces and from all parts of the country we hear of increased business activity, and of the projection of great enterprises. There is a bustling awareness of strong forces at work.
