To activate these forces the government must, as I think it intends to do, first of all create a situation which encourages the greatest possible degree of free enterprise. I do not use this word in a trite sense. I mean freedom in every possible way for the manufacturer and the individual to take advantage of the growth which is upon us. Secondly, it must reduce government controls of all kinds, including any taxes which have been thought to be crippling, and thus allow the greatest possible choice of freedom of movement both for the businessman and the individual worker.
I think the people in this country want the greatest measure of social security for those not able to look after themselves, but I do not believe they want social services so extensive as to stifle willingness to work or to discourage adventure. They want wages high enough to provide for present needs, and for savings and investment for the future.
It seems to me that industrial growth depends upon several factors, the first of which is a firm, constant and stable government policy to encourage risk capital and investment in a growing country; secondly, a high degree of skill in engineering and in industrial and personnel management- and this I believe we have; third, stable and sound relations between labour and capital; and fourth, a skilled and mobile work force. And it is about this latter that I wish to speak at some length, and to emphasize its importance as strongly as I can.
It is my opinion that our experience in wartime demonstrated, without any doubt whatever, that an industrial economy is impossible without a large body of skilled craftsmen. Whatever skills we may have with respect to finance and management, without skilled workmen we face a hopeless task. We know that for years before the first war, and between the two wars, we were content to extract from the land, sea, forest and streams the raw materials which formed the bulk of our exports. Now we demand the establishment of secondary industries. We have grown tired of purchasing


back our own raw materials in the form of manufactured articles and we find ourselves in the competitive markets of the world where sentiment does not exist.
To secure a fair share of these markets for our manufactured goods and, at the same time, maintain a high standard of living as expressed in a high scale of wages, we must produce cheaper, better and more attractive goods than our competitors. This cannot be done unless we reduce the cost of production by producing goods in greater quantities, in shorter time. If we are to prosper industrially, and if we insist on the five day or shorter work week, then we must produce more in those five days than we formerly did in six days, and without any decline in quality or appearance.
At the turn of the century, when Canada emerged from a mainly agricultural economy and began to lay the foundation of a great nation with a balanced economy, it was possible only because we were able to draw upon Europe, and chiefly Great Britain, for the majority of our skilled craftsmen- we trained none of our own, or very few. The United States had done the same. Those days are over. The two wars ended all that. The trained mechanics in the older countries are needed in their own countries. So now we must do one of two things:-[DOT] first, institute a vigorous campaign for the recruitment of skilled workers from Europe- and I know how far we would get if we suggested that-or, secondly, train our own.
There is no choice here. In the meantime until we can train our own we must approve an immigration policy which is selective and which will bring to this country those immigrants who can best fit into the industrial Canada that is to be. I think the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill) is doing just that.
Mr. Speaker, because I have mentioned immigration, I hope I do not offend the rules of the house, if I revert to an incident, or a series of incidents, concerning a supposed statement by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration at a meeting we both attended in Victoria during the Easter recess. Because this matter has been raised in this debate, by others, 1 think I may have the privilege of adding a word.
I certainly have no desire, nor is it my place, to defend any minister or, for that matter, any member of this house, for something he actually did say. That is his responsibility. But when I know for a fact, having been present at the time, that the statement, or the implication of any such statement, which has been attributed to the minister, definitely was not made, then I think it is

my duty to stand up in this house and say so. When I first saw the comments in the press, and statements had been made in this house -there was a good deal of hilarity about it because, Mr. Speaker, we did return to the house on the first day in rather a jovial mood -I thought hon. members were having a joke at the expense of the minister. But, sir, the matter has gone beyond a joke and 1 am compelled to say that in the interests of us all this unfair and unjustified attack upon the minister, which appeared in the press from many parts of the country, and even in editorial comment, should be answered. May I put it to my colleagues-and I am reading this because I do not want my words to be misinterpreted-this is a matter which affects us all. I know it has been said that we on this side of the house suffer from the occupational disease of being wrongly quoted; but only today we had two hon. members on the other side of the house rise in their places and complain about the same kind of thing. But that is not the case today because in no newspaper article that I have seen has any statement appeared in quotation marks, except one or two words, and then a gap. What is increasingly common, as we all know, is that in newspaper reporting, particularly of the kind of meeting that we were attending, a young reporter, in his desire to shorten his report, puts in his own words what he thinks you say. We have all suffered from that kind of thing at times.
On the whole, the newspapers do exceptionally well, but in this case they slipped. Many papers in Canada jumped on the bandwagon. What happened was simply this. A meeting had been arranged in the Oak Bay high school, at which I, as the representative of the constituency of which Oak Bay is a part, was to be the speaker. I found that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was to be in Victoria on business, and I persuaded him to speak at the meeting, which he did, and he made a jolly good speech, too. He did speak about immigration and he did mention Canadian babies, but not in the way it has been reported. Let me end this by reading an editorial which appeared in the Victoria Daily Times of Saturday, April 16, written after the adverse publicity in the eastern press, and by a man who was present at the meeting:
What Mr. Pickersgill said:
Mr. Pickersgill's speech in Oak Bay a few nights ago apparently has become something of a cause celebre in national politics. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has been made the victim of a gross distortion in some newspapers.
He was quoted as saying, in effect, that native-born Canadians are superior to foreign immigrants. He said just the opposite, as the news report in the Times recorded next day.
The Budget-Mr. Fairey
The Oak Bay audience which heard him will remember that, choosing his words with obvious care, he said that he was an unrepentant believer in "the cradle" as the best method of increasing the nation's population. He immediately added that he did not mean to say for a moment that Canadians were superior to foreign peoples and hoped he would never be so foolish as to suggest such a thing.
He argued only that a child born in Canada could be adjusted to the ways of Canada more rapidly and completely than a foreigner who must learn an entirely new way of life. But as the cradles of Canada could not produce all the people needed in our under-populated country it was necessary to encourage immigration, which he is doing.
Few Canadians will disagree with a statement so obviously sound. Reported as it was delivered it would cause little comment and general approval. But Mr. Pickersgill reaches Ottawa to find himself quoted in the eastern press as announcing a crude racialist theory of Canadian superiority, which was the last thing in his mind.
Even though he denies such a statement in parliament, even though some newspapers have quoted him accurately, many Canadians who do not read the news carefully no doubt will continue to believe the original distortion.
This is the final paragraph, and the most important:
For this some unknown newspaper reporters are solely responsible. Their newspapers should be the first to offer Mr. Pickersgill a public apology and a full, accurate report of what he actually said in Oak Bay.
I led up to a suggestion that we had a choice in preparing for a great Canadian industrial economy by choosing between instituting a vigorous immigration policy for trained mechanics and training our own, but I got sidetracked onto this other thing.
I have given it as my firm opinion on more than one occasion that Canada must look to its own for its skilled workers. It is pathetic to ponder on the meagre efforts now made in this regard. Our universities are crowded with first-class students. The applied science faculties are crowded to capacity. Day and evening classes are offered at most of our universities in business administration, management, salesmanship and so forth. But what are we doing for the basic need, the skilled craftsmen who translate the ideas and the plans of the engineer into tangible goods? We talk very boastfully of projects such as Kitimat, steel mills on the Pacific, pulp mills running into millions of dollars, the Frobisher scheme, the great industries around Edmonton and tremendous factory expansion schemes in the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Where are the skilled men to come from to man all these expanded industries? Please remember that it is the unskilled man who is first unemployed. Moreover, to take advantage of these expansions, the labour force must not only be skilled but it must be mobile.

The Budget-Mr. Fairey
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) breaks his heart over the plight of miners in the province of Nova Scotia, who are facing, as they must, a dying industry there. They cannot be left gazing at a closed mine; they are too valuable. Men used to hard work and anxious to continue at it must either be trained for new jobs and moved where the jobs are, or be trained for jobs in industry which may be induced to locate in their own particular districts. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, surely this is important enough, vital enough and urgent enough to be considered a federal responsibility, as it affects the whole of Canada.
What has been done? Well, I am not going to be too long over this because I talked about it during the last session. Assistance to the provinces has been provided over a period of years. First of all, there was the Technical Education Act of the 1900's, which provided $10 million over the period of 10 years, and that was the end of that. Then the depression forced the establishment of a number of vocational or shop training schemes in improvised shops for the most part, and these, together with the provincial technical vocational shops, formed the backbone of the war emergency training program and later the rehabilitation program for the veterans of the war. But, in 1942, this parliament passed the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which is a permissive act. It simply authorizes the minister to conclude agreements with the provinces further to assist vocational training. It tied together a number of agreements which had been in effect and authorized the minister to continue. The main agreement, which is called the vocational schools assistance agreement provided $10 million as capital grants; that is, for buildings and major equipment, and $20 million to be allotted at the rate of $2 million a year for 10 years, to be used for maintenance and operation. That agreement expired in 1953 and has been renewed for one year. That is the thing that is causing us concern at the moment. Why was it renewed for only one year? It was renewed for one year to give the federal government an opportunity to look over the situation and decide what is the best thing to do.
I have spoken this afternoon on the importance of training a skilled labour force and I want to suggest what the federal government ought to do. Some people have interpreted the action of this government in renewing the agreements for one year only as a warning that the end of federal assistance is in sight. I urge the contrary view. Surely the accomplishments of the past and the needs of the future demand, not a curtailment of federal


assistance but a considerable increase if a skilled working force of our own people is to be able to man our expanding industry.
Just look around, Mr. Speaker. With the exception of a few schools like the Halifax technical school, the Montreal technical school, the Ryerson Institute in Toronto, a new school in Winnipeg, the Manitoba Technical Institute, the Calgary Polytech and the Vancouver Vocational Institute, we have not adequate training facilities in Canada. The rest of the schools of this type in Canada are simply small industrial arts shops and, as I say, these technical schools are not fully equipped to properly supply the demands which will be made upon them.
We have no school in Canada like the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the California Tech, and dozens of others in the United States. None of the schools we have is big enough or properly equipped for the task which faces it. There are not enough of them.
Here is another point which is rather important. We have a committee on manpower working under the Department of Labour, and there is also an advisory committee on apprenticeship training. During the past session the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) asked our approval for a measure to rehabilitate the physically handicapped, the basis of which was rehabilitation training. Where are those people going to be trained? Unless we stimulate the building and equipping and expansion of our vocational training facilities the provinces will be unable to carry this load alone.
This type of school is the most expensive to equip, to man and to operate; this is entirely beyond the capacities of the cities and the municipalities. I have mentioned the mobile nature of the working force that will be required and because of that I think it is a federal responsibility to assume part of the load in this regard. If there is any justification for federal assistance in any field, I submit that this is that field.
Furthermore, any agreement which the federal government may make with the province must be on a long-term basis. No city, no province can plan for education, certainly in the technical field, on a year to year basis. I was bold enough to go into the conference the other morning when the provincial premiers were making their initial addresses. I heard one say that there must be agreements for at least five years, but in my view five years is too short. I would go further and say that there should be a permanent arrangement.

Furthermore, any funds which are allotted should be adequate. I realize that that is a very loose term. I know we have had $10 million in the last 10 years for capital account, but I submit that $10 million would not do much more than build one school. There will have to be more money for capital account and for equipment and then assistance must be provided for the operation and the continuance of the work of these schools.
Lastly, and I think this is a most important thing, the funds allotted should not be merged into a general subsidy. I was a member of the vocational training advisory council, and I have also been a civil servant. I know that in a desire to simplify administration it is quite easy to suggest that it would be better to lump all this enormous number-it is an enormous number-of federal grants into one grant, and say to the province, "Here, take this and administer it yourself".
My answer is that that should not be done, for the simple reason that unless the federal grant is earmarked for a particular purpose the chances are that once it gets into the provincial treasury it will not come out in the same way and for the purpose for which it was allotted.
Therefore I am pleading that any financial arrangements made between the provinces and the federal government in connection with vocational training and technical assistance should be such that the assistance given by the federal government should form a separate fund and be kept separate from any general subsidy.
Lest I be thought to be one-sided, lest it be thought that a person interested in technical education has no interest whatever in other kinds of education, lest it be thought that one is either intellectual or not-of course I disagree with that entirely-I want to say that it was a matter of great satisfaction to me, and I am sure to all of us, to hear the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on Thursday last that it is still the intention of the government to recommend to parliament the establishment of the Canada Council.
While I have stressed the importance of training a skilled work force, and while I urge its vital importance, that is not to say that the more intellectual pursuits are not of equal importance. This council will be concerned with the arts, letters and sciences and it can do much to raise the cultural standards of our people so that both forms of education or training may march side by side, in no way antagonistic the one to the other but each contributing in its own way to the growth and development of a rich and satisfying way of life.
The Budget-Mr. Harkness

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to carry on my part in this debate in the traditional manner by taking up a totally different subject. During the past two or three weeks I have been reading editorials which have appeared in some of our newspapers dealing with the budget, and I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has also. I would think that probably as a result of that reading he may be having a few doubts as to how good the budget is, although he certainly seemed to have no doubts on budget night. I should like to read from these editorial comments briefly. The first is from the Vancouver Sun of April 6 and it reads:
Economic experts may now speculate about the minister's reasons for bringing down a deficit budget for what he expects to be the most prosperous year in the nation's history. Mr. Harris himself didn't say . . .
Our own guess is that Mr. Harris kept mum because it would be too hard to supply a rational explanation.
The last thing I pretend to be is an economic expert. However, one does not need to be an economic expert to see some of the irrational aspects of this budget. One of the basic premises from which the minister proceeded to make his calculations and estimates in regard to what the gross national product would be and so forth was that the poor grain crop last year in western Canada was largely responsible for the decline in the gross national product, that it had had a generally depressing effect on the economy of the country and therefore was responsible for the deficit.
To a quite considerable extent that is a demonstrable fallacy. It seems to be government policy to blame the weather last year in the west for any economic difficulties which are being experienced at the present time. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) set the pattern for this when speaking in an earlier debate. He said that the poor western grain crop last year was completely responsible for any difficulties in which the farmers found themselves, for the general economic picture, and so forth. In other words the Minister of Finance was simply picking up that assertion of the Minister of Agriculture and making it one of the basic premises on which he based his budget calculations.
At that time, in the previous debate, I pointed out that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was completely wrong. I pointed out that last year's bad crop had very little effect on the cash position of the farmer for the year just past and that it would make its effect felt in this present

The Budget-Mr. Harkness year 1955. When the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke in this debate I notice that he took up the same point and pointed out that this assumption made by the minister was quite wrong.
As the budget is based, to quite a large extent, on this demonstrable fallacy, one is [DOT] led to look with the greatest of suspicion on all of the conclusions that are drawn from that basic fallacy. Particularly, one is bound to look with the greatest possible doubt on the estimate of what the gross national product will be for this present year and therefore on the estimate of government revenues which will be produced.
As a matter of fact, the poor crop in 1954 will make itself felt in this coming year, 1955, and will cause the western farmers' income to be greatly reduced both because of the fact that the crop was low in number of bushels and because it was of poor quality and will therefore bring a low price. The result of the combination of these factors is that the farmers in the west are going to have considerably less money in their pockets this year than they had last year, rather than more, and less money to put in the general stream of the economy. Unless a great deal more wheat is sold this year than was sold last year, the western farmers' income just cannot help being greatly reduced, with all of the consequent general depressing effect on the economy which the minister spoke of in his budget address.
In view of all this and in view of the poor prospects at the present time for a large increase in wheat sales this year, I think the minister's estimate of a gross national product of $25J billion for this year-rising, as a matter of fact, to a rate of $26 billion by the end of the year-is quite unrealistic. Similarly I think that the estimate of his deficit as being only $194 million is equally unrealistic. It is extremely difficult to see how this deficit will not be much more than $194 million. It seems to me that in his budget the minister would have been much more honest had he taken account of what the actual economic situation is at the present time and what it is bound to be as far as the western wheat farmer is concerned instead of saying: If we have a good crop our gross national product will be up, our revenues will be up and so on, and therefore I am budgeting for a deficit of $194 million. The easiest thing in the world to do is to make yourself look foolish a year from now by making predictions about what the deficit is likely to be or not to be. However, barring a war or something of that sort, I shall be greatly surprised if the minister does not have a much greater deficit than $194 million.

As the amount of grain produced and marketed, together with the price at which it is sold, has such a marked effect on the Canadian economy and therefore on government revenues, I propose to go into the present wheat situation in some detail. At this point I may say that I find that it is hard to get at what the wheat situation is at any particular time. There is a terrific mass of statistics which more or less overwhelm one when one starts trying to wade through them. In addition to that fact, the wheat board will not give out the sales figures for the current year. Hence all you can do is make your own estimate in connection with those figures, on the basis of the disappearance of wheat-figures for which are given out-and things of that sort.
Again, in addition to that, the statements issued by the government and by the wheat board from time to time seem to vary in order to make the situation appear better than it is or to make the situation appear to be what the government wants people to believe it is. An example of this sort of thing has occurred quite recently. I refer to Hansard for Friday, January 21. On that day the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) why it was that Canada's share of the over-all wheat market had dropped while the share of three other countries had increased. As reported at page 403 of Hansard the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied as follows:
They may be in the records, but my hon. friend is looking at shipments rather than sales . . . It is really the sales that count.
In other words the minister at that point was maintaining that the thing that was important was the sales of wheat and that the fact that exports had dropped was a matter of no importance. He was maintaining that you really must base your calculations on the sales. Last year, when the sales of wheat were quite low, in the committee on agriculture I tried to make that very point, namely that in order to get any idea what the return to the farmers was likely to be or what the general grain situation was likely to be, we must look at the picture of sales. But, Mr. Speaker, if you look at the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on agriculture and colonization for last year at page 139 you will find what was said by Mr. Mclvor who was then giving evidence, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce was sitting beside him. After I had tried for a considerable length of time to impress upon him this point that sales were important and so forth, Mr. Mclvor said this:
A. Mr. Harkness does not agree, but I think the figures we should look at are the exports figures. Once you get the sales you get into a variable thing that does not give a true picture.

In other words, last year when exports were better than sales, the only thing that was important really was the exports; sales just gave you a false picture. This year when the minister says that sales are much better than they were at this time last year-but we do not know what the figures are because the wheat board will not give them out-he says that sales are the important thing and that we should not pay any attention to exports. All these things merely serve to confuse the picture and, as I say, make it difficult to find out what the situation actually is.
Subsequent statements by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the acting minister, in answer to questions asked by members of the house, were to the effect that the sales this year are expected to be as good as or better than they were last year. It will be necessary for them to be much better. That is, if we get a reasonably good crop this year, it will be necessary for them to be much better. Otherwise our carry-over of unsold wheat will reach a new record and farmers will be able to deliver little, if any, of this year's crop; I refer to the 1955 crop. Sales for the 1953-54 pool period-that is the last pool period, the one from August 1, 1953 to July 31, 1954-were only 271-5 million bushels. The carry-over in 1954 rose at one time to a high of 740-7 million bushels. That was in March a year ago. At March 31 this year, that carry-over had been reduced but it was still 621-5 million bushels or nearly double the average carry-over for the period from 1945 to 1953. In other words, we still have an extremely large amount of unsold wheat. We have a big carry-over. A reasonably good crop in the present year of 1955, a crop of 400 million to 500 million bushels, will mean an increase in the carryover. At a sales rate of 270 million bushels a year, which is what the minister hopes we will reach, and provided we have a reasonably good crop of 400 million to 500 million bushels, the carry-over will increase to over 900 million bushels. If we get a crop of over 600 million bushels such as we had in 1952 and 1953, it will bring the carry-over up to over a billion bushels.
Every farmer naturally hopes he will have a good crop this year. He dares not hope otherwise, but having in mind the present carry-over, the prospect of what a good crop will do to that carry-over, plus of course the fact of the very large carry-over in the United States, he is very apprehensive as to the price he will receive for the wheat he will grow this year and the wheat he still has on his farm from the crops of last year 50433-207
The Budget-Mr. Harkness
and the year before. He is also very apprehensive as to how much of this year's crop he will be able to deliver.
Without any question, it is a very serious situation and the government deals with it simply by turning out soothing statements. That is all they do about it. They make statements which really give a wrong impression as to what the situation is. At the same time they talk about anyone who attempts to state what the actual situation is as being unpatriotic. They say he is going to spoil our markets abroad as though the people who are buying our grain do not know the situation far better, I suppose, than anyone in this house. In other words, the government says: Oh, you should not mention our large carry-over; it will discourage foreign buyers from buying. Such talk is completely ridiculous.
What the government should do is to face the situation and make greatly increased efforts to dispose of our wheat. They should also be doing something about increasing storage space, a matter I have mentioned several times during the past three or four years when we were having big crops and there was a storage problem.
I should now like to turn to another aspect of the wheat picture, and the most important one in a way as far as the individual farmer is concerned. I refer to the amount of money the farmer actually gets into his hands, which of course goes from there into the general stream of the economy through payment by him for food, clothing, machinery and so on. The amount of money received by farmers was very materially reduced during the 1953-54 pool period compared with the 1952-53 period. I should like to note what the figures were. In the 1952-53 pool the farmers received, by way of initial, interim and final payments, a total of $940.5 million. In the 1953-54 pool they received by way of initial payments $535.8 million. The only way I can get at what they are going to receive in addition is by making estimates from the wheat board reports, and on the basis of these estimates I think the amount will be approximately $50 million. It will certainly not be very much more or less than $50 million.
When the farmers get the final payment, about which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has promised to make a statement shortly after he returns, they will have received $585-8 million, or a reduction of $364-6 million in one year. It is no wonder that sales of farm machinery, machines, trucks and all sorts of other things are very considerably reduced. The farmers have received that much less money to spend. For

The Budget-Mr. Harkness the sake of accuracy, I should mention that these prices are basis Fort William. Therefore the farmers' freight costs would have to be deducted from these figures so that instead of the amount being $364 million it would perhaps be $350 million. The farmers have received that much less than they did the year before.
With respect to payment to farmers for wheat delivered, settlement has of course been made for what they delivered in previous years, but for 1953-54 they received an initial payment of $1.40 a bushel, less freight of course, and an interim payment of 10 cents a bushel. The interim payment of 10 cents a bushel means that they received another $39-8 million. Therefore out of the estimated figure of $50 million to complete payment there now remains only a little over $10 million which means, as far as I can see, that the final payment, which has been looked forward to with a great deal of eagerness and anxiety, is likely to be between two and three cents a bushel. Unless I have completely misread the wheat board report

 and I am fairly sure I have not-unless some money is to come from the government in the form of an advance or wheat remaining on hand is taken at a price considerably above the current market price, the final payment, as far as I can see, would only amount to between two and three cents a bushel which, rather than being welcomed with open arms, is going to be welcomed with great gnashing of teeth.
To turn to the future, the prospects for the 1954-55 pool period are much worse. That is the period we are in right now. In other words, it is the pool period in which the poor crop grown last year is being marketed plus, of course, wheat from the other crops still unsold. The estimated western wheat crop in 1954 was only 274 million bushels. Most of it was of low quality. As a matter of fact, a good deal of it was No. 5, No. 6 and feed wheat. This wheat would bring the farmer an average of less than 90 cents a bushel as far as the initial payment is concerned. That is all the cash he would actually get in his hands. Some would get quite a bit less than that depending on their distance from the head of the lakes.
Thus it is easy to see that the cash received for wheat in the 1954-55 period will be much less than last year. It just has to be a great deal less because the amount of wheat is small, it is of low quality and the price is down. This of course will have a consequent effect on the general economy.
I should also like to say something about a fairly general misconception which exists that the price of wheat is reasonably good.


This is certainly not the case as far as returns to the farmer are concerned, particularly compared with the cost of the things he has to buy. The average price received for wheat sold in the 1953-54 pool year, the one just ended, was $1.75 a bushel, basis Fort William. But what did the farmer get? That is quite a different story. I calculate that the carrying charges on the 1953-54 pool wheat sold were 21 cents a bushel, according to the wheat board report. One can calculate that the charges would be around that figure because most of this wheat was in storage about 18 months. The elevator charges would come to about 15 cents a bushel and as the wheat was bought from the farmers with borrowed money the interest charges would come to another 5, 6, or 7 cents a bushel. Therefore, taking elevator charges and interest charges, you get a cost just for carrying the wheat of something in the neighbourhood of 21 cents a bushel. This will bring the price down immediately to $1.54. From this, of course, has to be deducted the freight which would average probably 17 cents a bushel. In my own case I think the freight from my shipping point is 22 cents a bushel. The freight from some points in Manitoba would be much less than that, but I believe the cost of freight would average about 17 cents a bushel. This brings the price down to $1.37.
Now, in terms of the 1935-39 dollar, this means that a farmer is getting not more than 65 cents a bushel at the most for this wheat. This price was considered so ruinous in the thirties that as a matter of fact the Bennett government, which receives so much abuse from hon. members to your right, put a floor under wheat of 90 cents a bushel in 1935. This would be equal to a price at the present time, basis Fort William, of $2 per bushel. In other words, the price the farmer is getting in terms of real purchasing power is less now than it was in the period so frequently referred to as the dirty thirties. This is a point which I believe most people, particularly in the eastern part of this country, have failed to realize.
The returns per bushel on wheat for the 1954-55 pool, that is for grain grown last year, show an even grimmer picture. The result will not be anything like this price of $1.37 per bushel. For example, I delivered two loads of wheat from my last year's crop which made up the 300 bushels I was allowed to deliver last fall to the elevator. One load was No. 5 and it netted me 85-5 cents per bushel. The other load was No. 6 and I received 83-5 cents per bushel. This was my initial payment. On the basis of the final payment made last year I would say we are going to be very fortunate if it comes to

15 cents a bushel this next year. In other words, I think I will probably be lucky if I get a total return of $1 per bushel for that wheat. A great deal of last year's wheat crop was No. 5, No. 6 and feed-in other words very low priced wheat. The people closer to the head of the lakes, of course, will receive a few cents more.
In any event, I do not think there is any question but that the returns to the farmers on a great deal of last year's low quality crop will not be sufficient to cover expenses. Under these circumstances how much prospect is there of the farmers buying large quantities of new machinery, trucks, automobiles and such things, thus boosting the general economy of the country and improving government revenue for the year 1955? There is just no prospect of that. If we get a good crop this year, and everyone hopes we will, it will not help the cash position of the farmers in 1955 very much. The elevators are filled with grain, and they will be filled when this new crop starts to come off. Thus, the farmers will be able to deliver only an extremely small amount which will not enable them to cover their harvesting expenses. The cash position in 1955, therefore, will not be benefited to an appreciable extent even if we get the best crop we have ever had.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not preaching blue ruin. I am quite certain that western agriculture will come through these difficulties and that the grain farmers of the west will continue, as they have in the past, to be one of the mainstays of the Canadian economy. However, the economic picture for this year is anything but the rosy one which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) painted. I believe he would have been better advised to take this picture into account, rather than base his budget on vague hopes, and base his estimates on those hopes.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the speaker who preceded me, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), and particularly when he pyramided figures of wheat board costs of operation per bushel. He stated he was not too sure of some of his figures; but if he had examined the wheat board report for the crop year 1953-54 he would have found that 50433-207J
The Budget-Mr. Weselak the receipts of the board were 398,031,819 bushels. He would have found that the cost of operation, including carrying charges, terminal storage, interest and bank charges, handling stop-off and diversion charges, drying charges and administrative and general expenses totalled $35,767,299.77. It would have been a simple matter of mathematical calculation to arrive at a figure of less than nine cents a bushel as the total cost chargeable to farmers in that pool.
In entering this debate I propose to restrict my remarks in the main to aspects of the budget which relate to our international position in the matter of trade. Before doing so I should like to comment generally upon the budget as a whole and to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) upon the responsible approach he has taken in preparing his first budget and the capabilities he displayed in presenting it.
The past year has seen a drop in the gross national product of 2 per cent, which has reflected itself in loss of national revenues and a resulting deficit in the past year. This drop, as has been stated, was mainly due to a poor crop in western Canada which has resulted in a slowing down of economic activities by reason of the fact that farmers curtailed purchases last year when they saw their crop deteriorate owing to the weather. To help accelerate recovery from this situation, which in the past few months has shown signs of improvement, the tax reductions in the budget are welcomed; and while their effects may not immediately be obvious they will no doubt have the effect of encouraging economic expansion and stimulating business activity in this country.
I see nothing seriously wrong with limited deficit financing in times when a lift is needed to stimulate activity and relieve unemployment. Every prudent person believes in accumulating for the time when he may be short. From 1945 to 1954 substantial surpluses had accrued, when times were buoyant. Now it is only common sense if necessary within a limited degree to budget for deficits when economic conditions warrant such action. We have heard the criticism that we are borrowing on the future. It can be just as well said that we are cashing in on the past, when surpluses were budgeted for and did accrue to the treasury.
As to the relief given, income tax reductions will provide additional purchasing power. Added stimulus will be given to corporate investment by the slight reductions in corporation taxes. The reduction of the excise tax on automobiles will leave further purchasing power available and assist the automobile industry. Reductions in tariff items on agricultural items will also reduce
3263	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Weselak
the cost of farm operations. These concessions were well placed, and all will help the expansion of economic activity in the country and so promote employment.
In the amendment proposed by the official opposition we find the charge that the government has failed to recognize the serious position in which the Canadian farmer and other producers find themselves. I stated at the outset of my remarks that I intended to direct my remarks to our trade situation, which I presume is the item of government activity at which this charge is levelled.
In the course of this debate and others we have heard from opposition benches charges to the effect that Canada has lost her British market, and also to the effect that this government has callously ignored the difficulties of certain industries in which unemployment exists, and that it has failed to provide adequate work for these people and their employees.
The reduction of our sales to Great Britain has been the result of many factors. In the debate in reply to the speech from the throne I drew attention to the fact that the comparative prices of agricultural products laid down in England by other countries were substantially lower than prices existing in Canada for the same products. I expressed the opinion that this competition could only be met by export subsidies or substantial reduction in domestic prices.
There is however another reason for the drop in our exports to England, and this applies not only to England but to all countries with which we have trade relations. And that is the practical problem of balance of trade.
Our goods can only be paid for by buying the goods of others, in the field of international trade. The hard fact is that we either take goods in payment or cease to exist as a trading nation. We cannot eat 400 million bushels of wheat, consume $915 million worth of pulp and newsprint, or our mineral production. Unless we can dispose of this production we cannot pay the producers of these commodities and they in turn cannot pay those employed by them and those who service them and supply them with equipment and materials.
We have repeatedly heard the argument in this house "Let us bar foreign goods and make work for Canadians". This would be all very well if we were a self-sufficient nation and independent of world trade; but we are not and therefore must be realistic in our approach to the problem. And it is my observation that this government, in spite of most pressing demands from the opposition and many industries, has resisted,


in the interests of our Canadian economy, these demands for more protection which would have the effect of barring foreign imports and of increasing prices to con-sinners.
In specific cases and on particular merit, adjustments may be necessary and. advisable; but any broad blanket advocation of higher protection is certainly not in the national interest.
Particular reference in this debate has been made to the textile woollen industry and to the unemployment resulting from British competition, and the inference has been left to the effect that the government has given no consideration to this problem.
In all fairness, I believe that the record of this government in this regard should be brought to the attention of the public and in the limited time available I propose to deal with this matter.
On May 12, 1954, as a result of numerous representations from the woollen industry and those dependent upon it, the former minister of finance directed the tariff board to make a study under the Tariff Board Act of item 554b of the customs tariff, which provides for a tariff on woven fabrics composed wholly or in part of yarns of wool or hair n.o.p. a British preferential tariff of 20 per cent, and 12 cents per pound but not to exceed 50 cents per pound.
As a result of this direction, hearings were held in Ottawa and a number of plants were visited by the board and their economists. Appearing before the board were representatives of the Canadian industry, of the British wool industry, boards of trade of communities affected, agricultural associations, manufacturers, consumers and others. In all, 58 associations, companies and organizations submitted evidence or made representations.
The evidence indicates that those appearing before the board realized the seriousness of the woollen textile situation, sympathized with the workers who had lost their jobs, with the communities affected and with those who had invested their savings in the plants which have been closed. Nevertheless, it was the belief of many that the practice of helping a languishing industry by increased tariff protection, when other causes were the main contributing factors, was not sound.
In the direction to the board, in addition to requesting all relevant information concerning the woollen industry, the minister also requested all relevant information concerning as well the implications for the Canadian economy of imports of wool fabrics from the United Kingdom.
In the evidence submitted it was shown that our imports from England in 1952 were

roughly $360 million; in 1953 $453 million, and the latest information indicates that in 1954 they had dropped to $392 million. Of these amounts, in 1952 woollen textiles accounted for $29 million; in 1953 for $38 million and in 1954 to a lesser amount averaging in recent years about $33 million a year, or about 12 per cent of the total earnings from sales of British goods in Canada. Our exports to the United Kingdom fell in 1954 to $652 million from $665 million in 1953.
The board therefore had two directives: first, to determine whether tariff item 554b was the cause of the difficulty in the wool cloth industry and, secondly, to inform the government regarding the implications a tariff increase might have on our trade relations with the United Kingdom.
In the hearings before the board, the industry and its supporters including suppliers of material, technicians, labour unions and some municipal authorities, argued that the real cause of the disaster that had overtaken the industry lay in the devastating effect upon prices in Canada of competition from British producers and the increased volume of their shipments to Canada. On the other hand, opposing parties, particularly the national council of clothing manufacturers of Canada, the United Kingdom wool textile delegation, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the interprovincial farm union council contended that although there were other causes, the major cause of the difficulty in the industry was the declining total demand in Canada for wool cloth, and that the import of British wool cloths, as such, was not the main cause of their difficulty.
The board report discloses that since 1948 there has been a drastic decline in the total consumption in Canada of wool fabrics, a drop from 47.5 million linear yards in 1948 to an estimated 31 million in 1954. In the war years and to 1948, demand was strong and the industry thrived, but by 1949 the demand began to decrease. The outbreak of the war in Korea, however, led to increased production and prices and by March, 1951, wool prices had risen three times higher than in June, 1950. This was followed by a drop in price by September of the same year of 64 per cent. Large inventory losses were sustained, weakening the financial position of the industry. In 1952 demand dropped still further, plants were forced to shorter time and employment declined considerably. In 1953, some improvement was noted which carried into 1954.
The report then proceeds to discuss the factors which contributed to the decline in
The Budget-Mr. Weselak demand, such as changes in type of demand, production of worsteds, cloths, woollens and blends.
In their reference to the 17 closed mills, the board expressed the opinion that their closing was probably due to a combination of factors, stating that there was no doubt that the management of some of the older mills, of which there were 11 closed, were not as alert and efficient as they should have been. Old machinery had not been replaced as it depreciated; often no salesmen were employed to meet competitive markets in recent years and, finally, they had failed to adapt production to changing demand.
The findings of the board regarding wages and employment were to the effect that in the industry labour is a substantial item in the cost of production. They found that despite substantial increases since the end of the war, wages were comparatively lower than those paid in other manufacturing industries, the average wage being 111.7 cents per hour in the industry as compared with 141.7 cents per hour for manufacturing generally. To meet the problem of high labour costs, production must be efficient. Manufacturers must take advantage of latest improvement in equipment to make possible considerable reduction in labour costs. The report indicates that full advantage has not been taken by the industry of technological changes which would have a marked effect in making the industry competitive.
The brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture points out that productivity in Canada per man hour over the past 30 years has increased about 2 per cent per annum compound rate. On this basis, the production per man hour in the woollen industry should have reached an index of 132 in 1953 instead of 111. It is significant to note that while the productivity per man hour in the woollen industry stood at 111 in 1953, the real wage index for the industry stood at 155.
In examining the financial position of the industry, the board found that from 1939 to
1950	the industry had been profitable. In
1951	and 1952 severe losses were evident in the companies examined and it was evident that a substantial portion of the industry was in serious difficulty. The closing months of 1954, however, showed an upswing in activity and it appeared that this trend would continue.
The report discloses that approximately 1,450 workers had lost their jobs as a result of closed mills, and estimates that 2,800 had been laid off in the period 1949 to 1953, many of whom had found other employment.
After examining conditions in the industry, the board report proceeds to cite and examine

The Budget-Mr. Weselak the causes of its present difficulty and classifies them under the following headings:
1.	Decline in the demand for cloth containing wool.
2.	Competition from synthetic fabrics.
3.	Expansion of production facilities in relation to markets.
4.	Merchandising policy of the industry.
5.	Competition from British wool-cloth exporters.
The board expressed the opinion that the decline in the demand for cloth containing wool had been the most important single factor contributing to the present state of the wool cloth industry, demand having dropped in 1952 by 42 per cent of the 1948 peak and risen in 1953 to a drop of 36 per cent. They attributed this drop mainly to competition from synthetic fabrics, which in many cases have replaced woollens, generally are less expensive and not subject to wide price fluctuations.
Regarding the third item, "expansion of production facilities in relation to markets", the board found that following the war, plants were in a run-down condition. Demand was still heavy, with the result that surpluses previously accumulated were used up to reequip and expand plant facilities in order to meet a market starved by war restrictions. When in 1948 demand decreased it was found that production facilities exceeded the market, competition for available markets increased, prices fell and only the most efficient producers could carry on, and some plants were compelled to close their doors, or operate on part time.
As to the styling and merchandising policy, the board report indicates that considerable criticism was levelled at the industry by manufacturers and consumers for their failure to change styles rapidly enough to meet changes in demand. Apparently, there has already been considerable improvement in the quality and style of many lines of Canadian production as a result of this experience, but markets were lost in the meantime.
Regarding merchandising, the criticism was -that the industry had failed in their promotional campaign of Canadian-produced woollen goods, particularly in making Canadian consumers aware of the quality and good -value of Canadian wool goods and in following up this campaign with a system of labelling to prevent misrepresentation. The report in all fairness indicates that until 1951 this was a minor problem, and that the Canadian manufacturer now realizes that he must ally quality production with an active sales policy if he is to hold his market.

The linal important cause of the industry's trouble, "competition from British wool fabrics", was the main reason for the inquiry since, in its final submission to the board, the wool cloth industry had maintained that, owing to price competition from the United Kingdom industry, its continued existence was in jeopardy.
Of the total decline in the market from 1948 to 1954, which is estimated to have been about 16 million yards, Canadian production was decreased by 11-5 million and British imports by 4-6 million. In all sections of the market British imports had gained ground, but not to the extent that had been generally the belief, namely, 7 per cent in blends, 10 per cent in woollens, and 23 per cent in wool worsteds. This bore out and confirmed the board's deduction that much of the present difficulty was not the result of British competition but rather owing to the general shrinkage in demands for woollen cloths.
In examining the effective rate of duty, the board found that in 1954 the percentage of value for duty was three-tenths of 1 per cent lower than 1948, despite reductions in price, which would indicate that the 50 cent maximum tariff had become the governing rate in most cases, resulting in effect in a specific duty on the commodity. In view of these and other considerations, the board arrived at the conclusion that the effective rate of duty, per se, could not be considered as a cause of the industry's present difficulty, but on the other hand they did not deny that the competitive position of the British and Canadian industry had not changed since 1948.
As a matter of fact, the report points out that Canadian labour costs are 50 per cent higher than those in the United Kingdom, putting the Canadian manufacturer at a disadvantage whioh requires him to reduce labour costs by increased use of laboursaving machines, higher work loads and more efficient planning and operations. The industry is to be commended on recent reports to the effect that cognizance has been taken of this aspect of the problem and that it has been met in many ways.
The report concludes with the observation that rising wage rates and shrinking production have combined to increase the unit costs of Canadian cloth in recent years, with the result that in spite of a corresponding rise in British costs our competitive position has deteriorated.
In summarizing their report, the board had this to say on page 47, which I think is worthy of record, and I quote:
From the board's inquiry into the state of the wool-cloth industry, the following salient facts have emerged:

1.	The total demand in Canada for cloth containing wool has fallen drastically since 1948. The effects of this decline in demand, per se, appear to have been more severe on the woollen than on the worsted section of the industry.
Among the factors contributing to this shrinkage of the market have been:
(a)	the rise in wool prices, 1950-51, causing later inventory losses to the industry and, by the same token, initiating consumer resistance to increasing prices of wool clothing;
(b)	the growing competition of the domestic synthetic industry, which competition seems to be impinging more on woollens than on worsteds;
(c)	the competition of consumer durable goods for consumers' dollars, resulting in consumers spending a decreasing proportion of their income on clothes and personal furnishings.
2.	As a result of the fall in demand, the Canadian market for cloth containing wool has become increasingly competitive; moreover, in recent years British competition has been exerting a strong influence on the level of prices for wool cloths. This influence appears to be stronger in the worsted section of the market.
3.	Rising wage costs and shrinking production have combined to increase the unit cost of Canadian cloth in recent years. In spite of rising British costs this is still considerably higher than that of British exporters.
4.	The effective rate of duty on wool cloth has shown little variation since 1948 and, per se, cannot be considered a cause of the wool cloth industry's present malaise.
Three of the four facts above stated-the shrinkage in total demand, the downward trend of prices, and the rising costs of Canadian producers -when taken together constitute the background to the picture that presented itself as the board's inquiry progressed. They help to explain two further and resultant facts; that employment has fallen, and that some sections of the industry have been and still are in financial distress. Equally, however, they suggest at least that some mills which are responding to the challenging situation will continue to hold their own; and that among those which appear unable to do so further mortalities would seem inevitable.
Hon. members will recall that in December of 1953 Bill No. 29 passed through this house to prevent end of line dumping in Canada, particularly of textile goods. It passed against the vocal protest of some members and with considerable concern on the part of others. Many thought that this was a retrograde step in our efforts to increase our international trade upon which we are so dependent. Recognizing the fact, however, that this type of competition was almost impossible to meet and that the industry was in difficulty the bill went through and became law. The industry, however, felt this was not enough and the result was the reference I have referred to and the board's subsequent report which attributed the difficulty to internal competition in the main rather than to imports.
The Budget-Mr. Weselak
We have heard complaints in this house and in the country of United States nonadherence to the principles of GATT in its establishment of quotas and import restrictions. Usually the United States has good reason for these actions, and a great deal of consideration by their tariff authorities is given to each problem as it arises. The practice in Canada of referring these matters to the tariff board is to be commended and should be continued. Tariffs should not be imposed merely as a result of political pressures to the detriment of the country as a whole and this report is a classic example of the inadvisability of accepting the principle or theory that tariff protection is the only solution to a problem of this nature. This item is also bound by GATT and only the most serious considerations should result in its disturbance.
Hon. members may often wonder why western representatives, be they farmers, business or professional men, are and always have been advocates of low tariffs. The answer lies in the fact that we recognize our dependence on exports. We recognize the fact that this is not only a prairie problem but a national problem. We know that, if we are not able to find remunerative markets for our surplus production, the farmers' and primary producers' purchasing power is cut down. The effect in the cities, towns and villages in these communities is immediately apparent but it does not stop there; it moves to eastern Canada where much of the industry of the country is concentrated, and they too feel the pinch.
It can be said without hesitation that most of the economic difficulties experienced in this country today can be attributed to the decline last year of grain exports to England of almost $300 million and to a loss of crop value this year as a result of weather of a sum similar in amount. Our economy depends upon export of primary products and to a limited extent of raw materials and toward this end this government has done a tremendous job of saving GATT, which has served us so well in restraining other countries from indiscriminately imposing import quotas and prohibitive tariffs against entry of our products. The attitude of the United Kingdom may be gathered from a report in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 13 of this year, which states:
British Labour party leader Clement Attlee said today his party would favour Britain's re-entry into the international wheat agreement but only under certain conditions.
Mr. Attlee hinted that one of the conditions would be for the countries that sell Britain wheat to buy more goods from Britain.

The Budget-Mr. Weselak
And he is directly quoted as saying:
But we also want to sell goods. It depends on whether the people who want to sell us wheat are prepared to buy our goods.
Here we have one of the answers by a responsible statesman from the United Kingdom giving an indication of what an increase in tariff may do to our British market.
The woollen textile industry has asked the government of Canada to abandon its liberal international trade policy which it has been attempting to establish before and since the inception of GATT in 1948. They have asked that protection against British woollen cloth be increased so that British imports will be reduced, hoping that more Canadian wool cloth would be sold in Canada and less British and that more employment would be created in Canada for workers in woollen goods factories. They have asked for what appears to be a simple solution to a difficult problem.
The problem, however, is not that simple. The granting of protection, while it may have temporarily eased the difficulty, would not have provided the solution, and the report so indicates. The real problem to be faced by the industry is the decreasing demand for the product, resulting mainly from competition with synthetics and the need for increased efficiency to levels higher than those achieved in recent years.
Supposing this government had acceded to the request of the industry for a prohibitive tariff, what would have been the results? In the first place the price to the consumer would have increased with the result that there would have been a further swing to synthetics, a swing which was experienced when woollen fabrics reached their high early in 1951. Any decline in the consumption of woollen goods would affect the Canadian industry to a greater extent than it would affect imports. Earlier in my remarks I pointed out that from 1948 to 1954 the market declined by 16 million yards; of this decline the Canadian industry lost 11-5 million yards and importers 4-6 million yards. It is therefore doubtful whether an increase in tariff would help the industry. On the other hand, it might well have the effect of further reducing consumption to the extent that the industry would be in far more serious trouble.
Secondly, granting higher protection to the woollen industry would lead other industries to consider such action as a strong precedent and pressures would be exerted by many industries experiencing difficulty for further tariff protection. Canada has been a leader

in more liberal international trade policies, and any change in our position would strengthen the force in countries which seek to reverse the trend toward greater freedom of international trade.
And, finally, the problem of shortage of dollars which at present limits British purchases in this country is not an academic one, as is well illustrated by the British Labour party leader's remarks which I have just quoted. It is a cold hard fact and something which is well known by the farmers of Canada and other producers who look to the British market to sell their surplus products. A reduction in British exports to Canada as a result of higher tariffs would put into reverse a policy which aims at bringing the day nearer when the pound sterling would be freely convertible and British import restrictions removed. It might be of interest to members to know that the textile industry in England is also in difficulty. I have here a Reuters dispatch which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on April 22, which is headlined:
Lancashire Mills Fight to Survive.
Fewer wheels are spinning in the mill towns of Lancashire, where Britain's industrial revolution was born a century ago.
Unemployment is mounting.
Cause of the trouble is increasingly stiff competition from India and Japan, who learned many of the techniques of mechanized textile production from Lancashire.
Their goods, produced with a lower labour cost, are underselling Lancashire textiles overseas and even on the British home market.
Extended stoppages which began before Easter affected nearly 40,000 textile workers and there are widespread fears the unemployment will increase.
Many workers are leaving the industry fearful that unemployment will be chronic. The cotton board disclosed recently that in two months this year 4,000 textile workers left to find more secure jobs.
Indications are that many more plan a switch, even if it means taking lower wages.
The industry as a whole is critical of the Conservative government for not taking action on proposals by employers and trade unions to counter the effect of foreign competition.
But some relief was afforded this week in the budget which cut purchase tax on household textiles.
Walter Lee, secretary of the Oldham operative spinners' association trade union, said: "Confidence in the trade is lacking. Buyers are holding off placing orders except on a hand-to-mouth basis".
Here we have the type of criticism levelled at a Conservative government which a Conservative opposition in Canada sees fit to level at the Liberal administration.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would draw the attention of the house to the closing remarks of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture contained in their brief to the tariff board, which I believe touches the root of

the problem and suggests a possible remedy. I quote now from pages 27 and 28 of the brief:
As we said in our opening remarks, we fully realize the seriousness of the present woollen textile situation. We sympathize with the distress of workers who have lost their jobs, of small towns which have felt the loss of business from unemployment and of businessmen who have invested their savings in these plants which have been closed. In spite of this we do not believe it is sound to attempt, by increased tariff protection, to restore the industry to its post-war high volume of activity.
Up to this time the usual way to help a languishing industry has been to increase its tariff protection. However, we believe that it is time a completely new approach is made to problems of this nature. We believe that where it can be shown that due to fundamental and rather rapid changes in economic conditions an important industry is in serious distress, then the government should accept some responsibility to aid the industry, and especially the employees and communities adversely affected, to reorganize on a sound basis to meet the problems of the changed situation.
There' are probably a number of ways in which this responsibility can be discharged. We will suggest one possible line of approach here.
It may well be that careful examination will show that some of the plants now closed would be able to re-establish themselves in the same towns by producing products in which they have a greater comparative advantage than in woollen cloth production.
We would point out that there are precedents for government assistance in the reorganization of industries which face fundamental and permanent changes in economic conditions. An example of one is the re-organization of the apple industry of the Annapolis valley of Nova Scotia, which we have cited.
Higher tariffs are a burden on consumers every year. Government financial assistance for reorganization on a sound economic basis need only be provided once. Such a policy we believe would be in the national interest and very directly in the interests of the employees, the employers and the towns which are presently in distress.
We put this suggestion forward for consideration believing it to be a more reasonable and sounder solution to the problem than either the proposal of higher protective tariffs or a policy of allowing the economic law of international comparative advantage to take its full toll of an ailing industry.
A lesson might possibly be taken by industry from a Chicago industrialist who appeared before the ways and means committee of the United States congress, which comment appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on April 8, 1954, as taken from the Globe and Mail. The comment reads:
A Chicago industrialist who has found a stable market for his products against Japanese competitors who pay only one-eighth of his labour costs, Charles H. Percy, laid bare for the ways and means committee of the congress at Washington the story of his company's progress in cost-cutting, product improvement and maintenance of profits, in the face of severe competition from Germany, Japan, England, Switzerland, Austria and Belgium. In one instance his company's competitive bid on tenders open to the world for camera lenses still would have been lowest-and profitable-without the allowance made for tariff protection.
The Budget-Mr. Regier
As a manufacturer of photographic equipment, Mr. Percy's firm has had to meet all the post-war hazards to international trade in their most severe form. It has not been content with revolutionary reforms in production techniques at home. It also has engaged in a form of capital export which shares with foreign collaborators the advantages of those reforms. Annual sales of the company are in excess of $40 million-and he still wants congress to go all the way in the Eisenhower freer trade program.
The climax of Mr. Percy's statement was that these results arose directly from the influence of severe competition, and that it is doubtful whether the new techniques of his firm ever would have been developed without that spur. He now frankly welcomes the opening of the United States market to all comers in his field. If he cannot compete in a certain line, he will abandon its production and let the foreign producer have the market. He did just that in one instance, after taking a loss of a million and a quarter dollars. He holds that this course is good for his industry, for the national economy, and for the promotion of profitable foreign trade in general.
Mr. Percy's all-out advocacy of President Eisenhower's program for freer world trade is thus the result of practical experience as a successful world trader in one of the most competitive of all international industries. His story is one of the most impressive documents in the contemporary economic record. It is recommended without reservation to academic and practical economists, government planners of trade and fiscal policies and to industrialists generally. It is a complete answer to the problem of successful competition.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had prepared a talk on the contents of the budget. However, after hearing what to the people in my area is an announcement of such great importance this afternoon, I am pleased that a little bit of leeway is usually allowed in this debate to enable members to express a few opinions on other matters.
I should like to take this opportunity to express the appreciation of the people of my riding-and I think I also speak for the people of a goodly number of other ridings in the area-when I express our gratitude to the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Pickers-gill) for his statement this afternoon with regard to the four-cent letter rate in the Vancouver metropolitan area and also with regard to the Burnaby postal services. We therefore are now at the beginning of obtaining an equal deal as compared with the people of the metropolitan areas of Toronto and Montreal. We feel that there are other services which these two older metropolitan areas are receiving; and in time I have no doubt that the members of parliament will be asking for those other privileges.
The four-cent rate means a great deal to the people of the immediate lower mainland. I spoke to one official of an organization that does not send out many letters. I refer to the New Westminster local of the International Woodworkers of America. Their

The Budget-Mr. Regier office management informed me that the four-cent letter rate would, if implemented, save them in the neighbourhood of $300 to $400 a year. This action means actually hundreds of thousands of dollars in savings to the people and the commercial concerns of the lower mainland. It is therefore no mean announcement that we heard this afternoon.
I realize that the decision was made only very recently, and I believe that the Acting Postmaster General has neglected to include in the area that he designated such smaller points as Port Moody, and Port Coquitlam. I have no doubt that he will see fit to include those points in the four-cent letter zone very shortly.
We have received something that is as important to us in Burnaby as is the four-cent letter rate. We have received recognition of the name of Burnaby. We never found much to complain about with regard to the postal services in our area. We feel that the administration has been good, considering the problems that have had to be met. We have every confidence that the administration will continue to be at least as good as it has been in the years gone by. In fact, the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) assured us some time ago that no changes would be made that would make any less efficient the postal services that we have been getting. It is now up to the deputy minister and his staff, as responsible civil servants, to see to it that the policy announced this afternoon by the Acting Postmaster General is carried out as efficiently and as speedily as possible.
I have not a doubt in the world that the mayor of New Westminster would have a good deal of advice to offer to the deputy postmaster general on how he is to administer the new set-up. However, in view of the deputy's experience during the past several weeks, I would advise him not to pay too much attention to the head of the city government in New Westminster. He might ask for the advice of the elected municipal officials of Burnaby which, after all, has almost three times the population of New Westminster. When the Acting Postmaster General was answering a question of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn), I think he was not aware of what happened last year when the postage rates were changed. At that time the rates of postage for the rural routes were not raised, and 1 hope I am safe in saying that the rural routes will also be getting the same four-cent letter rate. If he will look at last year's amendment to the postage rates I think he will agree with me.
I should like at this time to pay a heartfelt tribute to the role played in obtaining what we were after by the hon. member for


Bumaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode). Even though he recently threw a little bit of political mud at me back home, I nonetheless feel that he has rendered unique service as a Liberal member of parliament and I should like to hold him up as an example to a lot of other Liberal members of what a forthright rank and file member of the Liberal party is able to accomplish if he is willing to stand on his own two feet and not obey the dictates of the party machine.
