speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend to say that is most kind of him and I appreciate it very much.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here was a case where a political machine, whose spokesmen were the mayor of New Westminster and, I regret to say, an hon. member of the other place, was doing its utmost to undo the worthy efforts of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. I know that the people back home are not going to forget easily how the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond finally won out after hewing honestly to the line on this matter. I think a great deal of credit is also due to the South Burnaby board of trade who have worked in very close co-operation with the two members of parliament from Burnaby. I know that the North Burnaby board of trade will also be happy about the institution of the metropolitan postal system. In my view Burnaby, as an entity in Canada, has at last been born. It is a new Canadian baby, if you like, and you will be hearing a lot about it in years to come.
I think I should also thank the hon. member for New Westminster for his co-operation and in return offer him my co-operation in some work he is attempting to do. At least, I hope he is attempting to do it. I refer to the cleaning up of the nest of Liberal corruption that exists in his city and has existed for quite a long while. In my opinion one reason why the Liberal party in British Columbia is rapidly going the way of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan is that the people there are fed-up to the teeth with the old type of pork barrel politics that has been responsible for keeping this government in office for so long. I only hope the day is not too far distant when the people of central Canada will also be thoroughly fed up.
I notice that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) is in his place. I know he is considering an auxiliary airport for the lower mainland of British Columbia. Someone has advocated that my riding might be the site of such an airport. I have the advice of the Coquitlam municipal council when I say

that I do not want an auxiliary airport in my riding. I shall be very happy if the Minister of Transport will agree to the demands of the member for New Westminster and see that such an airport is established in the riding of New Westminster.
Discussion so far in the budget debate has largely revolved around the subject of income tax. I believe the income tax was first introduced in Canada as an emergency measure during the first world war. However, after that war was over the income tax was not removed. That was the time I began to hear about such things as income tax, and I still remember the explanation given to me of what an income tax is. I was told that an income tax was a means whereby the federal government took money from those who had more than enough to meet their needs and used it in order to help that section of the population that had less than enough to meet their needs. I always looked upon that as a great thing and a worth-while measure.
When the second world war came we of course used the income tax for various other purposes. We used it to reduce the amount of consumer spending. We lowered the exemptions greatly in order to pay for the war effort as far as possible. However, when a single man earning $1,000 a year has to pay income tax today or a married man earning as little as $2,000 has to pay income tax, the tax has lost its original intent. It is no longer a tax taking money from those who have more than enough in order to help those who have less than enough. When you tax the below average wage earner in Canada you cannot say it is a tax used for the distribution of wealth in the nation. It is taking money out of one pocket of the taxpayer and, minus the cost of administration, placing the net returns in his other pocket. It is robbing Peter to pay Paul. I do not favour that type of income tax, and in levying it I think we should get back to its original intent.
I should like to say a few words about the reductions that have been announced. I fail to see why some people with incomes in the neighbourhood of $7,000 or $8,000 a year should receive a tax reduction of $100 or more whereas other people receive a mere $3, $4 or $5. I think the people who need a tax reduction most, who need the greatest number of dollars in their pockets, are the people in receipt of low incomes. I think the method adopted whereby much help is given to those who do not need help and very little help, if any, to those who need help has done nothing to add to the purchasing power of the Canadian people. If people with incomes of $7,000 or $8,000 pay $100
The Budget-Mr. Regier less in taxes next year they will not use the $100 to add to their purchasing power. If they do anything at all with it, they will add it to their savings. In my opinion raising the basic exemptions would have been much more equitable and would have served a much more useful purpose. All income tax payers would thereby have received an equal tax reduction and the purchasing power of the Canadian people would have been enhanced.
What about the tax reductions that have been given Canadian corporations? I maintain that the tax reduction granted is not going to help any plant or industry facing difficult times to remain open. After all, when corporations make no profit they do not have to pay income tax at all and when you reduce the taxes only for those corporations whose net income is over $20,000 a year, you are not helping one single industrial enterprise to remain in business. You are not supplying a single unemployed man with additional employment. You are not protecting the employment of any of those who are now employed.
These tax reductions to corporations also cause me at this time to protest as vigorously as I can the wholesale robbery that has been occurring on the Canadian scene as a result of what some people fondly call the plough-back method. You look at the financial statements of Canadian corporations, Mr. Speaker, and you will see that time after time corporations making a certain amount of profit will retain a half, or very often over half, of the net earnings. They pay out less than half to the shareholders. I feel that this is outright robbery of the rights of the short-term shareholders in Canadian corporations. The company says it is not paying dividends out as earnings would indicate it is able, but is withholding half the net earnings for the good of the enterprise. However, those who this year own that enterprise will not necessarily be the ones who will reap the fat earnings that may be dished out in later years because of this ploughback.
I feel that if it is not robbery of the shortterm shareholder in those companies, it is robbery of the consumer of the products the company has made because it is obvious the consumer has been charged more than he needed to be charged for the goods. If it is not robbery of the consumers of Canada, it is robbery of the workers who have worked in that enterprise and who have really, by the sweat of their brow, earned those profits and who have received wages that were much less than they might have received. I think that money for re-investment in Canadian business should be honestly
3276	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Regier obtained by anyone planning either expansion of existing business or the opening of a new business.
I should like also to express my opposition to the false belief that some Canadians seem to have that we can expand ourselves into prosperity. For a while many of us in British Columbia had the notion that as long as there was new investment capital coming in, we could expand ourselves into eternal prosperity. It is about as ridiculous a notion as a wheel of perpetual motion. It reminds me of the individual who is living beyond his means, and month after month has to add to the money he owes in order to meet his ever-increasing debts until he finally winds up in bankruptcy.
How could the little man have been helped on April 5 last? I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) said yesterday when he said he would have preferred to see some easing of the onerous sales and excise taxes. I believe the little man would have been more than happy if he had heard an announcement that the sales tax on clothing had been removed. I believe the tax on all forms of material needed for the construction of houses should also have been removed. I think the government might have helped the little man who has a modest home and who finds the real estate tax on his home is climbing year by year. It would have helped if the government had announced a policy of low interest rates to municipalities, thereby removing the need for loading homes with the necessary debentures to cover such social needs as paved roads, water works, sewers and so on.
I was pleased to note that at the meeting of provincial premiers with our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the governments of British Columbia and Saskatchewan both called for federal aid and participation in a public investment program to meet the rising social needs of the Canadian people. Unless this government is prepared to embark on a public investment program in co-operation with the lower levels of government, we shall find our provincial governments having to resort to ever-rising sales taxes. We will find our municipalities and educational authorities having to continue raising the taxes on our homes.
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, are sound money folk. We do not believe that money can be taken out of the hat or out of a printing machine. We are firmly convinced, and we have the highest regard for the rights of ownership. We believe that all the unsold goods in Canada are owned by somebody, and it is wrong to say we will make more 

money available unless we are fully aware of where we are going to get that money. You cannot add anything to the net purchasing power of the people by simply increasing the amount of currency in circulation. I think that is very simple economics, and has always been endorsed by the Canadian people. However, we do believe the purchasing power of the Canadian people can be vastly extended by having every Canadian who is willing and able to work at work turning out the goods that are necessary. We may think that we can ill afford the necessary $300 million or $500 million that a national health insurance program would cost us. However, having over 600,000 unemployed costs the nation far in excess of the cost of a national health insurance program.
We are also a party that believes in rigid economy and efficiency in government. Because of Liberal propaganda, word seems to have got around that the C.C.F. is a party that does not believe in economy in government. We in the C.C.F., who have such a great social program to offer the Canadian people, are keenly aware that if we are going to meet this obligation to the Canadian people, then the utmost economy and efficiency on the part of those who are handling public funds is necessary.
I should like to mention one other thing that I do not like about our income tax. I do not like this business of some Canadians paying at a different tax rate from other Canadians. Here again I was pleased to note that the premier of British Columbia, when he spoke at the opening of the conference, endorsed a resolution passed last winter by the C.C.F. national council, in so far as it relates to any provincial government that does not want to sign a tax-rental agreement. In that resolution he advocated, as we have done in this house, that the income tax rate should be the same throughout the nation. We feel that the citizens of any province that does not want to sign a tax-rental agreement should be permitted to deduct the full amount of their provincial tax from the federal tax, provided they are willing to admit that such a thing as the national interest exists, and that the over-all control of monetary and fiscal policy at the national level is necessary and that they will not exceed the limits of taxation imposed on other Canadian citizens.
Now, we feel that that is a policy that could have been sold to the people of Quebec. We think the people of that province want to be Canadians, and are just as good Canadians as any of the rest of us. We believe this policy would have been acceptable to them. However, in its wisdom this government chose to announce a unilateral decision

whereby it has now created two types of Canadian citizens, one of which is to have one set of income tax figures, and the other to have another set.
When I spoke in the house on January 12 some hon. members shouted the name of Maillardville. May I inform hon. members now that since that time I have held my finest public meeting at Maillardville, British Columbia. There were some 175 persons at the meeting which, I suggest, is an amazingly good turnout for a political meeting at this time. That meeting concluded in a most harmonious fashion, and I told the people there that as long as they were going to send me to Ottawa I was going to continue to fight, to the utmost of my ability, until I saw the day that their four and a half million fellow citizens, relatives and friends in the province of Quebec enjoyed just as high a standard of living as that of other Canadians. And I shall continue to do so, all misrepresentations notwithstanding.
In the few minutes left at my disposal I should like to speak about markets, because markets for our Canadian goods affect vitally our level of prosperity. I have here the daily bulletin released on April 26 by the dominion bureau of statistics, which shows a growing increase in our trading deficit with the United States and a growing increase in our trading surplus with the United Kingdom. I feel that this is a dangerous course, and that action must be taken to reverse the trend.
The United States buys from us only those goods they have to buy. I do not think the problem is any longer the simple one of free trade or high tariffs. I do not think that Canadians any longer can be classified either as high tariff or free trade citizens. However, if I were asked, I would say that so far as the United States is concerned I am a high tariff man; because I believe it is in the best interests of primary producers in Canada that we have a high tariff policy in our dealings with the United States. I am equally convinced that we should remove tariff barriers in our dealings with the rest of the world.
The rest of the world needs those commodities we have in surplus quantities- surpluses which are hampering our prosperity at the moment. I would like to see, if necessary, even an export tax on our shipments of raw resources into the United States. No longer can we afford to ship raw oil into that country to be refined over there and then sold back to us, thereby robbing Canadians of employment. I do not think that practice can long continue. While I am neither a free trade nor a high tariff man, I am a high tariff man when it comes to the
The Budget-Mr. E. Leduc United States and, if you like, I am a free trade man when it comes to the rest of the world, which requires these commodities we have in surplus.
I believe I have said about all I need to say on that subject. However, I would repeat my regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has not seen fit to raise the exemption levels for the payment of income tax. In my view the reductions he has given are badly distributed, in respect of both corporations and individuals. I feel he is making the rich richer and the poor poorer. He has made no tax concessions I can see that will help over half the population of Canada who pay no income tax. In my view, reductions in excise taxes on articles such as clothing would give at least some help to these people. I see no help for governments at lower levels, nor do I see anything to meet our growing need for social services in Canada. There is nothing for the unemployed- except relief, and the process of turning back to the miserable, hungry thirties. There is nothing to encourage trade so as to help the farmers of Canada, nor is there anything to encourage greater employment in Canadian factories. There is nothing to prevent growing economic enslavement of our nation to the United States of America.
Mr. Speaker, if this is a typical Harris budget, then I would advise the aspirant to the leadership of the Liberal party to apply for leadership in what I like to term the new, and yet so old, Liberal-Conservative party of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15, 1952 when I spoke in this house I asked the Minister of Finance for a tax reduction and, in the spring of 1953 I was greatly pleased to note that the government had decided to lower certain taxes.
In that same speech, I also stated that we should, in the near future, provide assistance for invalid people. At the last session, the government deemed it advisable to enact legislation to that effect, legislation which must be accepted by the participating provinces.
In the last few months the revenue of the government has diminished somewhat on account of crop failures last year and the loss of foreign markets. If we succeed in selling our products on the markets of the world, and that is the problem at present, everything will be back to normal and our revenue will increase.
In spite of the gigantic works undertaken this year, the government has been able to
3278	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. E. Leduc alleviate the burden of the taxpayer, thus leaving him more money for various purchases and giving him some encouragement.
Increased capital investments for the development of our natural resources will also alleviate unemployment-a problem which has been so often in the limelight during this session-and will endow the nation with new wealth.
In spite of this temporary unemployment situation we have reason to look to the future with confidence. Our confidence will increase with the lowering of taxes-of which I will speak-and the vanishing of gloomy pictures such as those that have been painted concerning the present situation.
The government is not wholly responsible for the present unemployment because it cannot alone remedy completely such a situation; economic forces must be favourable and everyone must be willing to co-operate toward its solution. With the help of Providence, which we should seek, we will succeed, but without it all our efforts will be in vain.	,
The debate on the annual budget is an important event anxiously awaited by all taxpayers. The budget can bring about an improvement or a lowering of the standard of living, according as to whether taxes are lowered or increased.
During the previous years when inflation was a major consideration in daily life, the government had looked to compulsory savings and even increased taxes as a means of controlling it. In this way inflation was satisfactorily brought under control, while surpluses were accumulated in order to reduce the national debt in such a way as to deserve general admiration throughout the world.
In the last three years this country has had to go to considerable lengths to organize its defence and fulfil its obligations under the North Atlantic treaty.
These efforts must no doubt continue, but at a somewhat reduced pace, due to suspension of hostilities in Korea, which is such as to provide us with reserves out of our war production. The latter must of necessity be limited, as is evidenced in the budget.
At this moment I am showing my interest in the budget by bringing forward a few suggestions based on several years' experience in the preparation of municipal budgets, smaller in size and simpler than that of the government of this country, but large enough, nevertheless, to convey a general impression of its practical application.
I will draw upon my experience in this field to talk about this question and should my humble suggestions appear worthy of


implementation, I will feel that I have contributed in some degree to the elaboration of measures which cannot fail to bear fruit.
First, a few words on the preparation, adoption and implementation of budgets.
Estimates are prepared by the officers of the various departments which submit them for approval to their respective ministers who, in turn, bring them to the attention of treasury board. In most cases the ministers involved assume that these estimates are necessary to administration.
It is to be expected that those officials whose duty it is to submit the items make sure that the amounts are sufficient, and in order to avoid any deficit they may submit estimates in excess of actual needs.
The taxation rates, which are based upon the total of the estimates, cannot therefore be reduced or can be reduced but little unless our national production increases. Since the increase will be very slight this year, the only way to lower our taxes was through deficit budgeting and a reduction in expenditures.
A perusal of public accounts for 1953 shows that no appropriation has been exceeded and that expenses in many cases have been far less than the amount provided. That is an indication in itself that appropriations were excessive.
A brief look at some items will support my contention. If we take for instance the Department of Agriculture we find the following:

To obviate the difficulty created by the fact that no appropriation can be exceeded, only the total amount of the appropriations of a particular service could be taken into account; it would be in order to make transfers from one item to the other provided that the total amount of the estimates for a particular service is not exceeded.

Thus, officials would not be tempted to try to get approval for larger amounts on each item for fear of a possible deficit on any of them, if it were possible to make transfers from one account to another.
Such a policy would reduce the estimates and would have every department control and administer funds on a scale much smaller than the present one.
These suggestions are made in a constructive way and in the light of practical experience gained in another administrative field which has been fruitful and which could not be but fruitful also in this field.
I make them in the hope that they may be used to ease the income tax burden.
On the other hand, if it is not advisable to spend more than the amount of the appropriation, with the difference to be made up through a transfer from another item of the same department which could have the amount provided reduced or from the total appropriation, and if it is deemed advisable to keep the present system, I think that, as far as taxes are concerned, the means of previous surpluses could be used to reduce taxes.
It will be said that these surpluses have been used to cut down our debt. Very well, but we must remember that this generation has been called upon to pay for three wars as well as for the cost of unemployment relief in the years 1933-39.
Therefore, would it not be fitting that the next generation, which will be more numerous and which will know a better standard of living, should look after that debt?
The coming generation and those that will follow will profit more than those of the last two or three decades from the benefits of social welfare available to them. So I think that they could very well look after the gradual reduction of that debt.
I am one of those who believe in the future of this country, and the present generation, which has toiled so hard, should get some respite; we should grant it that respite as far as it is possible to do so.
I expect that the federal-provincial conference will bring about a discussion which may dispel any misunderstanding or erroneous concept of the part to be played by the administration in the best interest of this country.
The Quebec provincial income tax was imposed as a result of a lack of understanding and we must try to find a basis for agreement.
If we are unable, in this country, to reach such an agreement, how can we hope to
The Budget-Mr. E. Leduc pacify hostile nations and bring about a world-wide peace?
The leaders of a country must trust each other, and it should be possible to smooth out or even avoid any difficulties that might arise by mutual, fair and reciprocal concessions and providing that the advancement of this country is put above all other considerations of a personal or purely regional nature.
A spirit of conciliation has arisen that should be beneficial to our country; the clouded horizon of yesterday is clearing up and a more enlightened optimism prevails. Let us consider our problems without acrimony and prejudice and we shall get to understand each other better and deserve the title of Canadian citizens who have at heart the progress and the interests of this country which should gain in stature and importance as well as in moral and material greatness.
Considering the 1955-56 budget that has been brought down, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is counting, for this fiscal year, on an increase in business and on a reduction of administration costs.
I congratulate him on this; it made possible a reduction of personal and corporate income taxes and he will probably avoid the expected deficit if conditions get somewhat better.
I am of the opinion that the reduction of certain appropriations would help to impress upon the officials of the various departments concerned the principle of thrift which would enable them to run their respective branches on their estimates, or thereabouts.
The most efficient means at our disposal to manage the country economically would be, I think, to try to reduce all appropriations that could be reduced, and there must be several of them, according to the statement I referred to a moment ago.

I was astonished to hear such a declaration, knowing that it is far from the truth. I desire to remind him that this percentage of 99 per cent comes from his own imagination, and is not borne out by the facts. As I look over the different municipalities in my own county and neighbouring counties, I can state to the hon. gentleman that this year Lachine has reduced its taxes 20 cents on the $100;

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson Dorval has reduced its taxes by 30 cents again this year. The municipality of Ville St. Pierre closed its financial year last year with a surplus of $20,000. Ste. Anne de Bellevue had a surplus. All the municipalities on the island of Montreal, except one, have had a surplus. The city of Montreal, according to the comptroller of finance of that municipality, had a surplus of over $1 million last year.
Looking at the provincial records for the year 1952, I find that in 1951 the revenues of the municipalities, that is the cities and towns, totalled $112,081,000, and for 1952, $114,902,000. Expenditures for 1951 amounted to $106,601,000, and for 1952, $113,358,000.
We have to take into account that capital expenditures were made amounting to $6,140,000 in 1951 and $5,641,000 in 1952. Had these expenditures not been made the surpluses would have been much higher. I have a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of March 24 which states:
Quebec's municipal corporations reported an increase in both revenue and expenditures during 1953 and a $35,000,000 increase in debenture debt.
The 1953 edition of municipal statistics, released today by the Quebec bureau of statistics, lists 1953 revenues at $163,503,000 compared with $146,315,000 in 1952 and expenditures at $157,063,000 compared with $114,896,000 in 1952.	.

The various departments would then endeavour to stay within the estimates, because if they ask for 10 per cent more than what is strictly needed, for fear of incurring a deficit, they would be tempted to spend the whole amount, whence the difficulty of avoiding expenses, that might be necessary in certain cases, but are superfluous in many others.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) represents part of the county in which I was born, Bruce, I studied the budget most carefully in the hope that I might be able to find a number of virtues in it. However, I think the only commendable feature that I have been able to discover is the venture into deficit financing which he has made, and before I conclude I hope to have time to say a little more about deficit financing.
I am afraid that I cannot go along with the hon. members who have congratulated the Minister of Finance upon having given some relief in the field of income tax. With the
[Mr. Leduc (Jacques Cartler-Lasalle) .1
majority of Canadian families being in a position where they do not pay any income tax, this is not the time to consider easing the burden of those who do pay income tax. I realize that members of parliament with their sessional indemnities will have a sizeable reduction, but believe me this reduction is not going to solve the problem that faces many this year.
A married man with two children receiving $2,500 a year will have a reduction amounting to $4 or approximately 8 cents per week. That really is not enough to get excited about. But I have examined four other groups. First, the position of those who receive $50,000 a year is going to be improved by $954 per year. We have not a very large number in this group, but the 1,840 who receive incomes of $50,000 or more receive a sizeable total income of $143 million. The income tax payer receiving $50,000 a year is going to have an additional $954 per year to spend. How sorry should we feel for the poor chap who has to pay $20,145 to the income tax authorities and must get along somehow or other on only $29,855 per year. That means that he is 50 cents short of having $100 per day for 300 days in the year. It seems to me that we should not shed any crocodile tears over a person who has that amount left to spend. Giving that person an additional $954 to spend is not going to help the unemployment problem at all.
Those receiving $100,000 a year are going to be better off to the tune of $1,954. After they have paid their scheduled income tax somehow or other they will have to balance their budgets on $163.60 per day. Those in the $200,000 per year group are getting relief to the tune of $3,904 and will have left after taxes $261.50 per day for 300 days in the year. The last group mentioned in the table, those receiving $400,000 a year, will be helped to the tune of $7,854. After paying their income taxes they will have left $419.38 per day.
I do not think that any member in this chamber can suggest with a straight face that people in these income tax brackets who are getting such substantial assistance are really in need of special legislation. I think this budget is going to be remembered for what it fails to do rather than for these minor changes.
I cannot think of any good reason why relief should have been given to corporations. While they do pay a sizeable amount in corporation taxes, the Bank of Canada in its most recent statistical summary shows in a chart that representative Canadian corporations-manufacturing, mining, finance, insurance and so on-are in a very healthy position.

This chart shows that after paying taxes their profits in the years since 1950 ranged from a high of $455 million to a low of $290 million. At the last of 1954 the profits after taxes were up to $337 million.
I submit that the minister should not bring in a budget without facing the fact that the net farm income in Canada has been declining at an alarming rate since 1951 in particular. I have the details of national accounts, income and expenditure, put out by the dominion bureau of statistics. The 1951 net income received by farmers amounted to $2,108 million; in the next year it was down to $1,860 million; the next year $1,616 million; and in 1954, $1,109 million. I submit that this alarming decrease in farm net income is having a most serious effect on all sectors of our economy and before I conclude I shall make some suggestions on which I feel the minister must act.
Over the week end I spent some time in a study of "Distribution of non-farm incomes in Canada by size 1951". I suggest to hon. members that they study this booklet showing the distribution of non-farm incomes. I have prepared a little table from this and these figures have been confirmed by Miss Podoluk, of the dominion bureau of statistics, who worked on this study.
I have arranged this table, an analysis of the distribution of Canadian family annual non-farm income among 265 representative families of two or more persons, according to the income groups. As to the income group from nothing to $2,499, 34-2 per cent of the families fall in that category. Out of 265, there would be 91. The average for the group would be about $1,500. The exact amount is $1,530. As to the second group, $2,500 to $9,999, 63-8 per cent fall in that category, or 169, with an average yearly income of around $4,200; or, to be exact, $4,176. As to the third group, over $10,000, 2 per cent fall in that category, or 5 out of 265, with an average annual income of $17,907, or nearly $18,000.
Hon. members might be interested in knowing just why I took the figure 265. That happens to be the number of members there should be in the chamber tonight if they were all here. I should like those who are here to forget the indemnity or any other income that members might have. I should like the members to picture themselves as being in the position of the average Canadian family. Here is how we would proceed to distribute that family non-farm income, two or more persons in the family. I might say that if we had the figures for the farm income, the picture would be worse, but this is bad
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson enough. If we could divide the chamber, we would take a block from just this side of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and of the government members in that row down to this side, 91 in the group, with an average income of $1,500 a year. Then the next group would, of course, comprise the majority. There would be 169 in that group and the average income would be roughly $4,200. That would leave us five down in the section where the independent members are. There are only five in that group getting $10,000 a year or more. The average would be $18,000 per year.
Mr. Speaker, here is one of the fundamental problems confronting the Canadian economy at the moment. If this government cannot find ways and means to get more purchasing power into the pockets of 34-2 per cent of the families in Canada who have an average income of $1,500 a year, I think they have failed to discharge their responsibility. If these figures were broken down to show those who had under $1,000, under $1,500 and under $2,000, you would have a more shocking picture still. But any family in Canada today getting $1,500 is in the position, if they pay rent, of not having enough money left to pay for their groceries, shoes, clothing or health services.
Coupled with these figures that I have just given, I should like to present the figures in connection with the consumer credit outstanding in Canada as recorded in the Bank of Canada's statistical summary. This is the issue of March, 1955; it is the one that has just been released. I think it is fairly obvious that with a third of the families in Canada receiving an average income of $1,500, with so many tempting advertisements urging us to buy radios, televisions, automobiles, fur coats and everything under the sun, there is bound to be difficulty. As a matter of fact, when you go into your grocery store now in Ottawa, you must decide whether you want a Plymouth car or a Pontiac car, trip to Hollywood or what-have-you. Most of the large grocery chains are engaged in a competitive give-away program in order to get people into their stores to get a car along with an order of groceries. In due course somebody will get a car. But while just Pontiacs and Plymouths are being offered now, if other storekeepers are going to keep in the running, they will be obliged to offer a Buick or Cadillac.
These charts at page 81 showing the consumer credit outstanding present what to me is an extremely disturbing picture. Charge accounts have increased from $370 million in March 1951 to $503 million in December,

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson 1954. As to instalment credit, retail dealers have increased their accounts from $166 million to $315 million and finance companies from $216 million to $480 million. Cash personal loans through the banks, the small lending companies and credit unions have increased from $394 million to $665 million. The totals have increased from $1,146 million in March, 1951 to $1,963 million in December, 1954. Taking the two things together, Mr. Speaker-with one-third of the families in Canada in the lower income brackets with an average income of $1,500, with living costs as high as they are, and with this alarming increase in consumer credit outstanding-I believe they suggest that there is trouble just ahead.
Unfortunately the bureau of statistics did not compile this sort of information before the war or prior to the depression in 1929 and 1930. But, as I recall it, one of the danger signals prior to the serious crash in 1929-30 was the large amount of consumer credit that was outstanding. As long as people receiving $1,500 can get storekeepers and small loan companies to extend them credit so that instead of spending at the rate of $1,500 a year they are able to spend at the rate of $2,000 or $2,500, it is fine so long as they can continue to increase their borrowings. But a time will come when those who are trying to live on a $3,000 income when their cheque is only on the basis of $1,500 will find that there is trouble ahead.
I therefore think it is only fair to ask what should be done. I commend the minister for introducing deficit financing. I think it is a subject that should be developed. I am sorry that there will not be enough time to present the sort of development this particular case deserves. However, I want to make it clear that I am not asking this government to adopt a socialist program. I am merely asking them to carry out a program which a capitalist government developed and practised during the war crisis. Let us see what was done in the war period. I have before me "Statistics and Information on Dominion Government Public Borrowing Operations from September, 1939 to December, 1945". I find that our total war requirements in 1939 amounted to $23 million; in 1940 they amounted to $246 million; in 1941 they amounted to $1,413 million; in 1942 they amounted to $2,402 million; in 1943 they amounted to $4,177 million; and in 1944, the all-time high, they amounted to $4,923 million. But hon. members will tell me this: Oh yes, but we were fighting for our lives then; we would do anything to save the world from nazi tyranny. That is quite right.


But I submit that in peacetime, if given a lead by this government, the Canadian people will put forth in the year 1955 the same sort of effort they were able to put forth in the year 1944.
These two fundamental problems are obvious to every Canadian. It is a tragedy that farm income should be down approximately 50 per cent to what it was four years ago and that 600,000 Canadians should be in the position where they cannot find jobs and are going to be receiving relief from municipalities, provinces or the federal government, or a combination of all three, when we consider the great resources of Canada, the achievements of the Canadian people during the war years, and the hungry people all over the world.
During that same period we managed to keep our non-war expenditures at fairly low levels. However, I was interested in noting that we did find money for unemployment and agricultural relief. We spent $49-9 million in 1939, $57 million the next year, then $34 million, $8-5 million, $5-3 million and $3-9 million. All through the period we were required to put aside some money for unemployment and agricultural relief. It is also interesting to note that the war saved the Canadian National Railways from a continuous record of deficit financing. Before the war the publicly owned railway was running in the red over $1 million a week, but come the war we were able to change the deficit to a very substantial profit.
Therefore I think the job that the minister should undertake now is to face the fact first of all that 600,000 Canadians want work and cannot find it and, second, that the Canadian farmers want to continue to produce maximum amounts of food for our own people and for hungry people all over the world. In a little pamphlet prepared by our national office I note that in 1952 stolen property apparently accounted for losses of something over $6 million, business failures $32 million, automobile accidents $77 million, wages lost through illness $159 million, salaries and wages lost through strikes and lock-outs $15 million, but losses of production through unemployment amounted to $1,235 million.
Here are some of the constructive, desirable things that we in Canada could and should do. If we would do them there would be no unemployment problem and no difficulty at all about getting the people to consume adequate food. I think it is as plain as A, B, C that if one-third of the families of Canada have an average income of $1,500 they cannot possibly consume desirable quantities of milk, butter, eggs, cheese, cereals and other

products. We should undertake to build
500.000	new homes. We should speed up construction of the trans-Canada highway. We should build more hospitals, schools, parks and recreational facilities. New industries should be established in depressed areas. Two million furnaces are required and a similar number of refrigerators. We need about 2 million electric vacuum cleaners,
1.500.000	telephones, 1 million washing machines, and about 2 million homes, rural and non-rural, need water and modem conveniences.
I have gone through government budgetary expenditure and have made a note of some of the politically popular and socially desirable increases the minister should include in the budget with a view to alleviating unemployment and winning the battle in which Canadians should be engaged. First of all there are our veterans. We have had previous discussions in the house regarding the position of the veterans of the Boer war, even the Riel rebellion, world war I and world war II. We are proposing to spend $234 million for those who have served this country. I suggest that an extra $200 million be placed in their hands because these people are in the lower income third who are not able to buy the things they would like to have.
The next item I should like to mention is the Colombo plan. I should like to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) in the position where he will eventually have as much money to spend as his colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney). I have been very careful not to suggest any reduction in our national defence expenditures. We have been told that the very large amounts we have spent on national defence have been a major factor in preventing a third world war. No one can prove that is right or wrong, but I am not going to argue about it. I think Canada can continue to have as many people in the armed services as we now have, continue to spend as much money on national defence as we are now spending and do these other things as well. We would still have a budget a good deal less than we had during the war years, and we would be in the position where we would have a million of our youngest and strongest people available to help with the constructive program I have suggested.
Then there is the question of grants to universities. This is one way the federal government can assist education without opposition from any of the provinces. Since we cannot get agreement with respect to general aid for education, I see no reason why we should not spend $100 million a year to aid
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson our universities. Since it costs the Minister of National Defence $65,000 to train a jet pilot, surely $100 million to train university students would not place any strain on us.
With respect to family allowances, I could not agree with the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) when he suggested this afternoon that the Canadian economy will not stand a doubling of family allowances. The argument he advanced today certainly applied when the family allowance legislation was before parliament in the first place, because at that time we were concerned about our war effort, but I submit that the family allowance expenditures of $383 million have been a major factor in making it possible for a great many people in the lower income brackets to have some money every month with which to buy food for their children. Therefore I suggest an increase of $400 million in family allowances.
As to old age assistance, here is a group who really must have additional help, and I suggest another $100 million. The next matter is health. I should like to be most generous to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I think he suggested at one time it would require $600 million to carry out the sort of program he had in mind back in 1945. I think we should have another $600 million to introduce an over-all national health program. This would not be in addition to what we are now spending for health but would merely mean that there would be comprehensive health services for all Canadians and our people would not have to worry about meeting such costs at a time when they are sick and unable to earn.
I have suggested an extra $100 million for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). Some concern was expressed this afternoon about the cutting off of the vocational training program that has been so popular throughout the country. The amount of $100 million would more than cover that. I do not have in mind pouring money into labour, to deal with the unemployment problem, but if the sort of program I have proposed is carried out Canada will not have any unemployment problem.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) needs more money. I notice that the net operating loss of the agricultural prices support board was only $3-5 million in 1950-51 and $1-7 million the next year. In the next two years the foot-and-mouth disease resulted in the amount increasing to $32 [DOT] 5 million and $37-8 million, but in 1954-55 the amount was down again to $3-2 million. There is nothing for the Minister of Agriculture at all in the proposed budget for 1955-56 for

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson his agricultural prices support. The Minister of Agriculture certainly should have $100 million in connection with his program for agricultural prices support. This leaves me with housing, and for the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) I put down $200 million. It must be recognized that in our slums in our cities and on our farms we have a large number of people living in housing conditions which are a disgrace to Canada in this year of 1955. We must not regard expenditure on housing as being money down the drain. Investment in housing is a permanent investment that people will enjoy for 20, 30, 40 or 50 years.
I have not left very much time to discuss the interesting problem of financing this sort of program. The total of these figures which I have run over very quickly is only $2 billion.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is a billion?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is a billion? That is a very good question. This amount is still less than half of what the Canadian people were able to raise and spend on our war effort alone in the years 1943 and 1944. If I had the figures available of the amounts of money we gave away during those years as mutual aid and assistance to the United Kingdom and our other allies, it would make the money which we are spending now under the Colombo plan and specialized agencies look very insignificant. I do not argue, Mr. Speaker, it would be possible to increase our income tax and our corporation tax to meet this particular type of budget. I believe the policy of deficit financing which the minister has introduced in a very mild way is quite sound. I think we need not worry about the amount of money that we owe to ourselves.
I notice that we have planned this year to spend $474 million for servicing our debt. Fortunately, most of this money is paid back to Canadians. At some time no doubt we will have to consider what we are going to do about the very sizeable national debt that Canada does carry. But so long as the percentage of the spendable money paid to service our national debt does not get out of hand, really we have nothing to worry about. Canada is in a very strong position to undertake a deficit financing program now. Wisely

enough, I believe, during the years immediately following the war the government put aside sizeable sums to reduce our national debt. There was some criticism from the Conservative party about maintaining very high tax levels when all the money was not being spent. I feel it was a sound principle to have substantial taxes and make substantial payments on the national debt when money was plentiful and goods were scarce. Now that we have unemployment on our doorstep, we need not have any worry about deficit financing in Canada getting out of control. I believe we could secure more money by imposing higher taxes on the higher income groups. But then again, there is not enough money left in that particular pocket to solve all our problems. By carrying out a policy of orthodox financing, as demonstrated during the years I have mentioned from 1939 to 1945, the Minister of Finance could introduce a budgetary program that would make him the real hero of our particular period. But the budget that he has introduced, with tax reductions for a very small percentage of the Canadian people, very small amounts for the people in the lower income brackets and sizeable amounts for the people in the higher brackets, contains nothing spectacular.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that with the two problems which stare us in the face, the problem in our own country of so many of our elderly people, the invalids, the war veterans, our farm people in a position where they just cannot get their hands on sufficient dollars to enable them to meet their reasonable responsibilities and enjoy a reasonable standard of living; when we think of the two-thirds of the people in the world who look at us maintaining 600,000 people in the ranks of the unemployed, I feel that Canada should and must give better leadership in solving our own problems and helping to solve world problems.
On motion of Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we shall take estimates, beginning with citizenship and immigration; northern affairs; then post office and justice.
